query.original_query: grammatical gender bias cross-lingual interference multilingual language models representation of objects

sub_queries.semantic_query: grammatical gender bias and cross-lingual interference in multilingual language models, representation of objects in the residual stream and attention heads, circuit analysis of gender features
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the representation of grammatical gender in multilingual language models, analyzing how object gender features are encoded across the residual stream and attention heads. Using causal tracing and activation patching, we localize factual recall of gender agreement to specific MLP layers and attention circuits, finding that gender features are distributed across multiple heads rather than localized to a single component. Our analysis reveals cross-lingual interference: when processing a sentence in one language, the model’s gender representation for an object is partially influenced by the grammatical gender assigned to that object in other languages it was trained on. We find that attention heads in middle layers exhibit polysemantic behavior, encoding both language identity and gender features simultaneously. Results show that this interference is asymmetric, with high-resource languages exerting stronger influence on low-resource language gender predictions. Our findings highlight challenges in achieving language-agnostic gender representations and suggest that current multilingual models rely on language-specific circuits for grammatical gender, limiting cross-lingual transfer.

sub_queries.semantic_query: grammatical gender processing in multilingual speakers, cross-linguistic interference in object representation, bilingual language control and neural correlates of gender agreement
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated the neural correlates of cross-linguistic interference during grammatical gender processing in highly proficient Spanish-English bilinguals. Participants performed a gender decision task on Spanish nouns while undergoing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Critical stimuli were nouns whose grammatical gender in Spanish (masculine or feminine) either matched or conflicted with the gender of their English translation equivalent. We measured the BOLD response in regions associated with bilingual language control and lexical retrieval. Results indicate that gender-incongruent trials elicited significantly greater activation in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) compared to congruent trials, suggesting increased inhibitory control demands. Additionally, representational similarity analysis (RSA) of multivoxel patterns in the left inferior frontal gyrus revealed distinct neural representations for congruent versus incongruent items. Findings support the hypothesis that non-target language grammatical features are co-activated during object representation, requiring domain-general executive resources to resolve competition. These results extend models of bilingual language control to the processing of grammatical gender, highlighting the role of prefrontal regions in managing cross-linguistic syntactic interference.

papers.title: Analyzing Gender Representation in Multilingual Models
papers.research_question: How is gender represented in multilingual models? Is the gender concept encoded in shared subspaces across different languages?
papers.core_contribution: Gender representation in multilingual models consists of both shared and language-specific components. The most dominant gender directions are shared across languages, enabling good cross-lingual gender classification, but language-specific directions prevent effective cross-lingual gender removal.
papers.conclusion: Gender representation in multilingual models is partially shared across languages, with the most salient directions being shared and less salient ones being language-specific.
papers.key_findings:
Gender classification using linear probes transfers well across languages (English, French, Spanish).
Gender removal using Iterative Nullspace Projection (INLP) does not transfer well across languages.
Gender subspaces are spanned by a few dominant directions that are shared across languages and other language-specific directions.
The shared gender directions are the most dominant ones (highest predictive power).
The partial sharing explains the discrepancy between transferable classification and non-transferable removal.
papers.limitation:
The study relies on a narrow, binary notion of gender, which does not reflect the full complexity of gender bias.
The analysis is limited to three languages (English, French, Spanish) due to dataset availability.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models were shown to allow for nontrivial transfer across scripts and languages. In this work, we study the structure of the internal representations that enable this transfer. We focus on the representation of gender distinctions as a practical case study, and examine the extent to which the gender concept is encoded in shared subspaces across different languages. Our analysis shows that gender representations consist of several prominent components that are shared across languages, alongside language-specific components. The existence of language-independent and language-specific components provides an explanation for an intriguing empirical observation we make: while gender classification transfers well across languages, interventions for gender removal, trained on a single language, do not transfer easily to others.

papers.title: Interpreting Gender Bias in Neural Machine Translation: Multilingual Architecture Matters
papers.research_question: Does the multilingual neural machine translation architecture impact the degree of gender bias?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language-specific encoder-decoders exhibit less gender bias than shared architectures, and proposes two interpretability methods based on source embeddings and attention to explain this difference.
papers.conclusion: The choice of multilingual architecture impacts gender bias in machine translation, and the proposed interpretability methods help explain why language-specific models perform better by showing they encode more gender information and have more diverted attention.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific encoder-decoders show less gender bias than shared encoder-decoders when trained on the same data.
Language-specific models encode more gender information in source embeddings, as measured by SVM classification accuracy.
Language-specific models have more diverted attention, allowing them to consider a broader context when predicting gender.
Bilingual systems vary in the amount of gender information encoded in embeddings depending on the target language.
Most gender translation errors involve assuming masculine occupations, which may be due to data imbalances and linguistic/cultural factors.
papers.limitation: The conclusions are based on the WinoMT benchmark, which has known downsides such as unnaturalness and logical failures, potentially affecting the results.
future_direction: Providing real-world data benchmarks to evaluate gender accuracy in machine translation systems.
Experimenting with more distant language pairs to see if the conclusions hold.
papers.abstract: Multilingual neural machine translation architectures mainly differ in the number of sharing modules and parameters applied among languages. In this paper, and from an algorithmic perspective, we explore whether the chosen architecture, when trained with the same data, influences the level of gender bias. Experiments conducted in three language pairs show that language-specific encoder-decoders exhibit less bias than the shared architecture. We propose two methods for interpreting and studying gender bias in machine translation based on source embeddings and attention. Our analysis shows that, in the language-specific case, the embeddings encode more gender information, and their attention is more diverted. Both behaviors help in mitigating gender bias.

papers.title: Monolingual and Multilingual Reduction of Gender Bias in Contextualized Representations
papers.research_question: How can we effectively reduce gender bias in contextualized representations using DensRay, and how is gender information distributed in BERT?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes using DensRay to debias contextualized representations, showing it performs comparably to prior methods, is more robust, preserves language model performance better, and enables multilingual debiasing.
papers.conclusion: DensRay is an effective method for reducing gender bias in contextualized representations, maintaining model performance, and can be applied multilingually.
papers.key_findings:
DensRay effectively mitigates gender bias on OCCTMP and association tests.
DensRay preserves language model performance on Wikitext-2 and GLUE tasks better than other methods.
Gender information is spread across all attention heads and most layers in BERT, with no single head responsible.
DensRay can obtain gender bias scores on token and sentence levels.
DensRay can be used for zero-shot multilingual debiasing (e.g., debias Chinese using English data).
papers.limitation:
Token-level bias scores work well for monolingual BERT but not for multilingual BERT.
The method focuses only on the gender direction and may not address biases from implicitly gendered terms.
future_direction: Investigate multilingual transfer of debiasing techniques more closely.
Investigate debiasing with non-binary approaches (beyond male-female binary).
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models (PLMs) learn stereotypes held by humans and reflected in text from their training corpora, including gender bias. When PLMs are used for downstream tasks such as picking candidates for a job, people's lives can be negatively affected by these learned stereotypes. Prior work usually identifies a linear gender subspace and removes gender information by eliminating the subspace. Following this line of work, we propose to use DensRay, an analytical method for obtaining interpretable dense subspaces. We show that DensRay performs on-par with prior approaches, but provide arguments that it is more robust and provide indications that it preserves language model performance better. By applying DensRay to attention heads and layers of BERT we show that gender information is spread across all attention heads and most of the layers. Also we show that DensRay can obtain gender bias scores on both token and sentence levels. Finally, we demonstrate that we can remove bias multilingually, e.g., from Chinese, using only English training data.

papers.title: Don’t Forget About Pronouns: Removing Gender Bias in Language Models Without Losing Factual Gender Information
papers.research_question: How can we disentangle and remove gender bias from language model representations while preserving factual gender information?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using orthogonal probes to disentangle and filter gender bias from contextual language model representations while preserving factual gender information, showing bias can be reduced without significantly harming language modeling performance.
papers.conclusion: It is possible to decrease stereotypical gender bias in language model representations while preserving factual gender information, without significant deterioration of the model's language modeling capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
The method decreases gender bias in profession names (measured by MSE) while preserving factual gender information for gendered nouns.
Filtering bias dimensions only moderately decreases masked language modeling accuracy on general text.
Preserving factual gender dimensions in the filter can improve pronoun prediction accuracy in coreference tasks by removing confounding stereotypical bias.
Probing identifies sparse dimensions in the embedding space that encode bias and factual gender information.
The method works on multiple transformer-based masked language models (BERT and ELECTRA).
papers.limitation:
The method does not remove all gender information, so downstream classifiers could still retrieve gender, making it unsuitable for tasks using gender-biased data.
The method does not fully remove gender bias; some bias remains in the representations.
The linear probe may not capture non-linear encoding of gender signals in the Transformer, and information might be recovered in subsequent layers.
papers.abstract: The representations in large language models contain multiple types of gender information. We focus on two types of such signals in English texts: factual gender information, which is a grammatical or semantic property, and gender bias, which is the correlation between a word and specific gender. We can disentangle the model's embeddings and identify components encoding both types of information with probing. We aim to diminish the stereotypical bias in the representations while preserving the factual gender signal. Our filtering method shows that it is possible to decrease the bias of gender-neutral profession names without significant deterioration of language modeling capabilities. The findings can be applied to language generation to mitigate reliance on stereotypes while preserving gender agreement in coreferences. 1

papers.title: Gender Encoding Patterns in Pretrained Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: How do pretrained language models internally represent and propagate gender biases? How do bias mitigation techniques and fine-tuning affect these encoded biases?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a consistent pattern of gender encoding in pretrained language models (early layers suppress, later layers amplify) and shows that debiasing techniques, especially post-hoc methods, are limited in altering internal representations, while fine-tuning reduces encoded gender information but may concentrate bias in the classification layer.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that gender bias is deeply embedded in pretrained language models and that current debiasing techniques are insufficient, advocating for proactive integration of fairness objectives during pretraining and targeted interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Gender information follows a consistent encoding pattern across encoder models: early layers suppress gender signals, while later layers amplify them.
Debiasing techniques, especially post-hoc methods, show limited efficacy in reducing encoded gender bias in internal representations.
Training-time Counterfactual Data Augmentation (CDA) is the most effective debiasing method for reducing gender encoding.
Fine-tuning on a downstream task (occupation classification) reduces gender information in the encoder representations, but may concentrate bias in the classification layer.
Larger models (e.g., BERT-large) tend to encode more gender information than smaller models.
papers.limitation:
Focus on gender bias in English-language biographies, leaving broader sociocultural and intersectional biases unexplored.
The study centers on encoder-based models; future work should validate findings in decoder-based architectures and multimodal systems.
The interplay between task-specific fine-tuning and bias propagation requires deeper exploration across diverse applications.
future_direction: Extend analysis to broader sociocultural and intersectional biases.
Validate findings in decoder-based architectures and multimodal systems.
Explore the interplay between fine-tuning and bias propagation across diverse applications.
papers.abstract: Gender bias in pretrained language models (PLMs) poses significant social and ethical challenges.Despite growing awareness, there is a lack of comprehensive investigation into how different models internally represent and propagate such biases.This study adopts an information-theoretic approach to analyze how gender biases are encoded within various encoder-based architectures.We focus on three key aspects: identifying how models encode gender information and biases, examining the impact of bias mitigation techniques and fine-tuning on the encoded biases and their effectiveness, and exploring how model design differences influence the encoding of biases.Through rigorous and systematic investigation, our findings reveal a consistent pattern of gender encoding across diverse models.Surprisingly, debiasing techniques often exhibit limited efficacy, sometimes inadvertently increasing the encoded bias in internal representations while reducing bias in model output distributions.This highlights a disconnect between mitigating bias in output distributions and addressing its internal representations.This work provides valuable guidance for advancing bias mitigation strategies and fostering the development of more equitable language models. 1

papers.title: The Birth of Bias: A case study on the evolution of gender bias in an English language model
papers.research_question: How do language models come to be biased in the first place, specifically regarding gender representation during training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that gender representation in language models is dynamic during training, with gender information becoming increasingly local in input embeddings, and that debiasing these embeddings can reduce downstream bias, but naive strategies may introduce new biases due to asymmetry.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of monitoring training dynamics to understand bias development and to design effective debiasing strategies that avoid introducing new biases.
papers.key_findings:
The representation of gender in the model is dynamic, with different phases identified during training.
Gender information is represented increasingly locally in the input embeddings of the model.
Debiasing the input embeddings can be effective in reducing bias in downstream tasks like semantic textual similarity.
There is an asymmetry in how the female and male genders are represented in the input embeddings.
Monitoring training dynamics helps detect such asymmetries and informs better mitigation strategies.
papers.limitation: Naive mitigation strategies may introduce new undesirable biases due to asymmetry in gender representation.
future_direction: Generalizing the methods to larger language models and the Transformer architecture.
Applying the approach to other languages and other undesirable biases.
papers.abstract: Detecting and mitigating harmful biases in modern language models are widely recognized as crucial, open problems. In this paper, we take a step back and investigate how language models come to be biased in the first place.We use a relatively small language model, using the LSTM architecture trained on an English Wikipedia corpus. With full access to the data and to the model parameters as they change during every step while training, we can map in detail how the representation of gender develops, what patterns in the dataset drive this, and how the model’s internal state relates to the bias in a downstream task (semantic textual similarity).We find that the representation of gender is dynamic and identify different phases during training.Furthermore, we show that gender information is represented increasingly locally in the input embeddings of the model and that, as a consequence, debiasing these can be effective in reducing the downstream bias.Monitoring the training dynamics, allows us to detect an asymmetry in how the female and male gender are represented in the input embeddings. This is important, as it may cause naive mitigation strategies to introduce new undesirable biases.We discuss the relevance of the findings for mitigation strategies more generally and the prospects of generalizing our methods to larger language models, the Transformer architecture, other languages and other undesirable biases.

papers.title: Gender Bias in Multilingual Neural Machine Translation: The Architecture\n Matters
papers.research_question: Does the chosen Multilingual Neural Machine Translation architecture, when trained with the same data, influence the gender bias accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the MNMT architecture impacts gender bias accuracy, with Language-Specific encoders-decoders exhibiting less bias than Shared encoder-decoder, due to more gender information in source embeddings and more diverted attention.
papers.conclusion: The MNMT architecture impacts gender bias accuracy, with Language-Specific encoders-decoders outperforming Shared encoder-decoder due to better gender encoding in embeddings and more diverted attention.
papers.key_findings:
Language-Specific encoders-decoders architecture exhibits less gender bias than Shared encoder-decoder when trained on the same data.
Source embeddings in the Language-Specific architecture encode more gender information than in the Shared architecture.
Attention in the Language-Specific architecture is more diverted (has higher coefficient of variation) than in the Shared architecture, which helps in mitigating gender bias.
Adding Russian to the language set increases the gender bias gap between Shared and Language-Specific architectures.
Manual analysis shows that most gender errors are due to assuming masculine occupations instead of feminine ones, with some errors having linguistic and cultural explanations.
papers.abstract:
Multilingual Neural Machine Translation architectures mainly differ in the
amount of sharing modules and parameters among languages. In this paper, and
from an algorithmic perspective, we explore if the chosen architecture, when
trained with the same data, influences the gender bias accuracy. Experiments in
four language pairs show that Language-Specific encoders-decoders exhibit less
bias than the Shared encoder-decoder architecture. Further interpretability
analysis of source embeddings and the attention shows that, in the
Language-Specific case, the embeddings encode more gender information, and its
attention is more diverted. Both behaviors help in mitigating gender bias.

papers.title: Locating and Mitigating Gender Bias in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the locations and generation mechanisms of gender bias in large language models, and how can it be mitigated effectively while preserving model capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: This paper integrates locating and mitigating gender bias in a unified framework, using causal mediation analysis to trace bias to bottom MLP and top attention modules, and proposes the LSDM knowledge-editing method to effectively debias while preserving model capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Gender bias in LLMs is generated by the bottom MLP modules and extracted by top attention modules; the LSDM method effectively mitigates this bias while preserving model capabilities and can be extended to unseen occupational pronouns.
papers.key_findings:
The bottom MLP modules acting on the last token of occupational pronouns and the top attention modules acting on the final word are primary contributors to gender bias generation.
The proposed LSDM method reduces gender bias by an average of 71.4% across tested models and datasets.
LSDM outperforms fine-tuning and counterfactual data augmentation baselines in debiasing effectiveness and in preserving model performance on knowledge and reasoning tasks.
LSDM mitigates catastrophic forgetting, maintaining model capabilities on seven proficiency test datasets.
LSDM can generalize to reduce bias in some unseen neutral occupational pronouns, though effectiveness is reduced for out-of-distribution cases.
papers.limitation:
The collective influence of model components on the output has not been extensively studied.
LSDM's effectiveness remains poor for occupational pronouns outside the distribution.
The method focuses only on gender bias in occupational pronouns; extending to a broader range of biases is future work.
future_direction: Delve deeper into the mechanics of the debias method to thoroughly understand and apply it to enhance the model's knowledge performance.
Extend the method to a broader range of biases beyond gender and occupational pronouns.
papers.abstract: Large language models(LLM) are pre-trained on extensive corpora to learn facts and human cognition which contain human preferences. However, this process can inadvertently lead to these models acquiring biases and stereotypes prevalent in society. Prior research has typically tackled the issue of bias through a one-dimensional perspective, concentrating either on locating or mitigating it. This limited perspective has created obstacles in facilitating research on bias to synergistically complement and progressively build upon one another. In this study, we integrate the processes of locating and mitigating bias within a unified framework. Initially, we use causal mediation analysis to trace the causal effects of different components' activation within a large language model. Building on this, we propose the LSDM (Least Square Debias Method), a knowledge-editing based method for mitigating gender bias in occupational pronouns, and compare it against two baselines on three gender bias datasets and seven knowledge competency test datasets. The experimental results indicate that the primary contributors to gender bias are the bottom MLP modules acting on the last token of occupational pronouns and the top attention module acting on the final word in the sentence. Furthermore, LSDM mitigates gender bias in the model more effectively than the other baselines, while fully preserving the model's capabilities in all other aspects.

papers.title: Causal Mediation Analysis for Interpreting Neural NLP: The Case of Gender Bias
papers.research_question: How can causal mediation analysis be used to interpret the internal mechanisms of neural NLP models, specifically to understand the role of individual components (like neurons and attention heads) in mediating gender bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a structural-behavioral framework based on causal mediation analysis for interpreting neural NLP models, and applies it to gender bias, revealing that bias effects are sparse, synergistic, and decomposable into direct and indirect effects.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis provides a useful framework for interpreting neural NLP models, offering insights into the internal mechanisms by which properties like gender bias flow from input to output through various model components.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias effects are sparse, concentrated in a relatively small number of model components (neurons and attention heads).
Gender bias effects are synergistic, with different model components interacting to amplify or repress their individual effects.
Gender bias effects are decomposable, with the total effect approximating the sum of direct and indirect effects, despite model non-linearity.
Larger models tend to exhibit larger gender bias effects.
The causal mediation analysis framework captures general patterns of causal structure in Transformer architectures, not just model-specific characteristics.
papers.limitation:
The experimental design focuses on gender bias in a binary setup, which does not account for a gender-inclusive spectrum.
Preliminary experiments with gender-neutral references (e.g., singular 'they') showed models have not learned these concepts well, and the setup suffers from confounders like plural 'they'.
Results for masked language models (e.g., BERT) are less clear, potentially due to differences in scoring multi-token continuations compared to autoregressive models.
future_direction: Applying the methodology to more gender-inclusive setups and other kinds of biases.
Using mediation analysis to guide the development of new debiasing methods that establish counterfactual fairness.
Exploring path-specific effects to identify exact mechanisms through which biases arise.
papers.abstract: Common methods for interpreting neural models in natural language processing typically examine either their structure or their behavior, but not both. We propose a methodology grounded in the theory of causal mediation analysis for interpreting which parts of a model are causally implicated in its behavior. It enables us to analyze the mechanisms by which information flows from input to output through various model components, known as mediators. We apply this methodology to analyze gender bias in pre-trained Transformer language models. We study the role of individual neurons and attention heads in mediating gender bias across three datasets designed to gauge a model's sensitivity to gender bias. Our mediation analysis reveals that gender bias effects are (i) sparse, concentrated in a small part of the network; (ii) synergistic, amplified or repressed by different components; and (iii) decomposable into effects flowing directly from the input and indirectly through the mediators.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language when processing non-English prompts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that multilingual language models like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate representations favoring English before shifting to the target language.
papers.conclusion: The evidence suggests that the abstract 'concept space' in multilingual transformers lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding linguistic biases.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate embeddings in middle layers decode to English versions of the correct next token, even when the input and output are non-English.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space (high entropy, no language), concept space (low entropy, English dominates), and output space (target language dominates).
The concept space is biased towards English, indicating an internal pivot language.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The token energy metric shows that latent embeddings have low energy in middle layers and high energy in later layers when the target language is selected.
papers.limitation:
Focus on the Llama-2 family limits generalizability to other models.
Tasks are simple and provide a highly controlled, toy-like context.
Limited understanding of the structure of the concept space in its original high-dimensional form.
The logit lens only grants approximate access to internal beliefs about output; other information remains hidden.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias changes when decreasing the dominance of English during training, e.g., by using different language mixtures or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks, including more culturally sensitive problems and popular use-cases.
Better understand and map out the concept space in its high-dimensional form.
papers.abstract: We ask whether multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language -- a question of key importance for understanding how language models function and the origins of linguistic bias. Focusing on the Llama-2 family of transformer models, our study uses carefully constructed non-English prompts with a unique correct single-token continuation. From layer to layer, transformers gradually map an input embedding of the final prompt token to an output embedding from which next-token probabilities are computed. Tracking intermediate embeddings through their high-dimensional space reveals three distinct phases, whereby intermediate embeddings (1) start far away from output token embeddings; (2) already allow for decoding a semantically correct next token in the middle layers, but give higher probability to its version in English than in the input language; (3) finally move into an input-language-specific region of the embedding space. We cast these results into a conceptual model where the three phases operate in "input space", "concept space", and "output space", respectively. Crucially, our evidence suggests that the abstract "concept space" lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding the biases held by multilingual language models.

papers.title: On the Encoding of Gender in Transformer-based ASR Representations
papers.research_question: How much gender-related information can we linearly erase from an ASR model and what are the implications of linear erasure?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that gender information can be linearly erased from transformer-based ASR models with minimal impact on performance, and reveals that gender is concentrated in the first and last frames in the final layers.
papers.conclusion: This work sheds light on how ASR models encode gender and paves the way to creating usable but speaker-blind embeddings.
papers.key_findings:
Gender can be linearly erased from all layers of Wav2Vec2 and HuBERT without model training.
Linear erasure has minimal impact on ASR performance, as shown by small changes in Word Error Rate (WER).
Gender information is concentrated in the first and last frames in the final layers of the models.
Fine-tuning affects gender encoding, localizing it to specific frames in the later layers.
The ease of gender removal in later layers is due to its localization in shared subspaces within the first and last frame positions.
papers.limitation: lack of non-binary gender labels in the datasets used
papers.abstract: While existing literature relies on performance differences to uncover gender biases in ASR models, a deeper analysis is essential to understand how gender is encoded and utilized during transcript generation. This work investigates the encoding and utilization of gender in the latent representations of two transformer-based ASR models, Wav2Vec2 and HuBERT. Using linear erasure, we demonstrate the feasibility of removing gender information from each layer of an ASR model and show that such an intervention has minimal impacts on the ASR performance. Additionally, our analysis reveals a concentration of gender information within the first and last frames in the final layers, explaining the ease of erasing gender in these layers. Our findings suggest the prospect of creating gender-neutral embeddings that can be integrated into ASR frameworks without compromising their efficacy.

papers.title: Do LSTMs See Gender? Probing the Ability of LSTMs to Learn Abstract Syntactic Rules
papers.research_question: Does the LSTM learn abstract grammatical rules for gender agreement in French, or does it rely on simple heuristics like clues from gendered articles?
papers.core_contribution: LSTMs can perform long-distance gender agreement in French but show inaccuracies on plural phrases without gendered articles, suggesting reliance on surface clues rather than abstract syntactic rules.
papers.conclusion: Gender agreement is a useful probe for investigating LSTM's linguistic capabilities and the extent to which they learn abstract syntactic rules.
papers.key_findings:
LSTMs achieve high accuracy on gender agreement tasks even with long distractor phrases.
Performance varies more on shorter phrases with gender attractors, contrary to human behavior where longer phrases cause more errors.
Models may rely on gendered articles for agreement, as shown by lower accuracy on plural phrases where articles are uninformative.
Gender agreement accuracy is robust across different contexts like noun-adjective and noun-passive-verb agreement.
papers.limitation:
The model's performance on short phrases with attractors deviates from human behavior, suggesting limitations in mimicking human language processing.
The study does not provide a mechanistic understanding of how LSTMs perform gender agreement.
future_direction: Characterize the role of articles and other gender indicators in agreement.
Explore gender agreement in contexts beyond noun-predicate agreement.
Investigate whether learnt gender rules generalize to novel nouns.
papers.abstract: LSTMs trained on next-word prediction can accurately perform linguistic tasks that require tracking long-distance syntactic dependencies. Notably, model accuracy approaches human performance on number agreement tasks (Gulordava et al., 2018). However, we do not have a mechanistic understanding of how LSTMs perform such linguistic tasks. Do LSTMs learn abstract grammatical rules, or do they rely on simple heuristics? Here, we test gender agreement in French which requires tracking both hierarchical syntactic structures and the inherent gender of lexical units. Our model is able to reliably predict long-distance gender agreement in two subject-predicate contexts: noun-adjective and noun-passive-verb agreement. The model showed more inaccuracies on plural noun phrases with gender attractors compared to singular cases, suggesting a reliance on clues from gendered articles for agreement. Overall, our study highlights key ways in which LSTMs deviate from human behaviour and questions whether LSTMs genuinely learn abstract syntactic rules and categories. We propose using gender agreement as a useful probe to investigate the underlying mechanisms, internal representations, and linguistic capabilities of LSTM language models.

papers.title: Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Neurons in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: How and where do multilingual language models encode syntactic agreement? Are neurons shared across languages and structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper extends causal probing to multilingual language models, finding two distinct layer-wise effect patterns for syntactic agreement depending on distance, significant neuron overlap across languages in autoregressive multilingual models but not masked language models, and that behavioral analyses underestimate masked language models' sensitivity to syntax.
papers.conclusion: Causal probing reveals distinct mechanisms for short- and long-range syntactic agreement in multilingual models, with autoregressive models showing more cross-lingual neuron sharing than masked models, and suggests that models encode syntax similarly across languages but with language-specific neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Two distinct layer-wise effect patterns for syntactic agreement: one for short-range (adjacent subject-verb) and one for long-range (separated by other tokens).
Neurons are shared across syntactic structures but not with semantic baselines, indicating abstract syntactic agreement encoding.
In autoregressive language models (XGLM), there is significant neuron overlap across languages, but in masked language models (mBERT), neurons are rarely shared across languages.
Neuron sparsity differs across structures (more sparse for short-range agreement) but not across languages.
Behavioral analyses likely underestimate how sensitive masked language models are to syntactic information because negative interference from other neurons masks strong syntax-sensitive neurons.
papers.limitation:
Limited to stimuli where subjects and verbs are single tokens, restricting the range of words and languages that can be studied.
Probing individual neurons may oversimplify because complex phenomena like syntactic agreement are likely encoded in sets of neurons.
future_direction: Developing methods for multi-token interventions and variable-length sequences.
Probing multiple neurons simultaneously to causally implicate model regions rather than individual components.
Investigating redundantly encoded syntactic information across neurons.
papers.abstract: Structural probing work has found evidence for latent syntactic information in pre-trained language models. However, much of this analysis has focused on monolingual models, and analyses of multilingual models have employed correlational methods that are confounded by the choice of probing tasks. In this study, we causally probe multilingual language models (XGLM and multilingual BERT) as well as monolingual BERT-based models across various languages; we do this by performing counterfactual perturbations on neuron activations and observing the effect on models' subject-verb agreement probabilities. We observe where in the model and to what extent syntactic agreement is encoded in each language. We find significant neuron overlap across languages in autoregressive multilingual language models, but not masked language models. We also find two distinct layer-wise effect patterns and two distinct sets of neurons used for syntactic agreement, depending on whether the subject and verb are separated by other tokens. Finally, we find that behavioral analyses of language models are likely underestimating how sensitive masked language models are to syntactic information.

papers.title: Using Artificial French Data to Understand the Emergence of Gender Bias in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether gender is ingrained in a word's representation or dynamically computed from context, and which characteristics of the training set affect an NLM's ability to capture gender information.
papers.core_contribution: Transformer language models do not necessarily amplify gender imbalances in training data, and gender bias can emerge even with balanced data. Gender information can be ingrained in word representations or dynamically computed from context.
papers.conclusion: The findings challenge the assumption that training data imbalance is the sole cause of gender bias and suggest that transformers are not inherently biased to reproduce frequent patterns. Future work will generalize observations to natural language data.
papers.key_findings:
For words seen in gendered contexts during training, gender is ingrained in their representations, allowing correct assignment even in ambiguous contexts.
For words not seen in gendered contexts, the model can infer gender from context, but performance is near chance if only seen in ambiguous contexts.
For epicene nouns, the model accurately assigns gender based on context, but in ambiguous contexts, it tends to assign the most frequent gender from training.
Word frequency affects gender assignment in ambiguous contexts, with higher frequency leading to better accuracy.
Gender distribution in training data does not have a substantial impact on the degree of bias; models can exhibit bias even with balanced data.
papers.limitation:
The use of probes introduces an additional system rather than directly studying LM behavior.
The findings may not extrapolate to real models trained on natural language due to model size and data differences.
The PCFGs are based on French, and gender expression varies across languages.
The work considers a binary gender system.
future_direction: Generalizing observations to models trained on natural language data.
Exploring more intricate PCFGs to support coreference resolution challenges.
Examining how model and dataset sizes impact experiments.
papers.abstract: Numerous studies have demonstrated the ability of neural language models to learn various linguistic properties without direct supervision. This work takes an initial step towards exploring the less researched topic of how neural models discover linguistic properties of words, such as gender, as well as the rules governing their usage. We propose to use an artificial corpus generated by a PCFG based on French to precisely control the gender distribution in the training data and determine under which conditions a model correctly captures gender information or, on the contrary, appears gender-biased.

papers.title: Are We Paying Attention to Her? Investigating Gender Disambiguation and Attention in Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How well do neural machine translation models integrate contextual gender cues for gender disambiguation, and how is gender information encoded in their attention mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Minimal Pair Accuracy (MPA) to evaluate gender cue integration in NMT, finding models often ignore cues in favor of stereotypes and that attention patterns differ for male vs. female cues.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals a persistent male-as-norm bias in NMT models, with attention mechanisms encoding gender cues asymmetrically, reinforcing the need for more nuanced evaluation and mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Models struggle to consistently leverage contextual gender cues for disambiguation, as shown by low MPA scores.
Models perform better for masculine referents and in pro-stereotypical settings.
There is an asymmetry: stereotypically female professions are easier to override with a masculine cue than the reverse.
Attention analysis shows that feminine pronouns elicit more localized activations, while masculine ones receive more dispersed attention in some models.
Different models exhibit different attention patterns: OPUS-MT has a single head in early layers, while NLLB-200 and mBART have more distributed patterns.
papers.limitation:
Analysis only considers binary gender due to constraints of the WinoMT dataset.
Inherent gender composition imbalance in the data makes it difficult to draw definitive conclusions for underrepresented scenarios.
future_direction: Future work to develop more inclusive methodologies that better reflect gender as a spectrum.
papers.abstract: While gender bias in modern Neural Machine Translation (NMT) systems has received much attention, traditional evaluation metrics do not to fully capture the extent to which these systems integrate contextual gender cues. We propose a novel evaluation metric called Minimal Pair Accuracy (MPA), which measures the reliance of models on gender cues for gender disambiguation. MPA is designed to go beyond surface-level gender accuracy metrics by focusing on whether models adapt to gender cues in minimal pairs -- sentence pairs that differ solely in the gendered pronoun, namely the explicit indicator of the target's entity gender in the source language (EN). We evaluate a number of NMT models on the English-Italian (EN--IT) language pair using this metric, we show that they ignore available gender cues in most cases in favor of (statistical) stereotypical gender interpretation. We further show that in anti-stereotypical cases, these models tend to more consistently take masculine gender cues into account while ignoring the feminine cues. Furthermore, we analyze the attention head weights in the encoder component and show that while all models encode gender information to some extent, masculine cues elicit a more diffused response compared to the more concentrated and specialized responses to feminine gender cues.

papers.title: Voice, Bias, and Coreference: An Interpretability Study of Gender in Speech Translation
papers.research_question: How do speech translation models assign gender to speaker-referring terms, considering the influence of training data patterns, internal language model biases, and acoustic information from input audio?
papers.core_contribution: Speech translation models assign gender to speaker-referring terms by learning broader masculine biases from training data and using first-person pronouns to access acoustic gender cues distributed across formant frequencies, rather than relying solely on pitch.
papers.conclusion: ST models learn broad masculine biases and use first-person pronouns to access acoustic gender cues from formant frequencies, demonstrating distinct mechanisms for gender disambiguation in speech translation.
papers.key_findings:
Models do not memorize term-specific gender associations from training data but internalize a general masculine skew.
The internal language model (ILM) exhibits strong masculine bias, but acoustic input can override these preferences.
Contrastive feature attribution reveals that models rely on first-person pronouns like 'I' to link gendered terms back to the speaker.
Acoustic cues for gender assignment are distributed across the frequency spectrum, with emphasis on first and second formants, not concentrated in pitch.
There is an asymmetry: feminine predictions rely more on acoustic cues, while masculine predictions rely more on internal biases.
papers.limitation: The analysis uses a binary gender framework, excluding gender non-conforming individuals.
papers.abstract: Unlike text, speech conveys information about the speaker, such as gender, through acoustic cues like pitch. This gives rise to modality-specific bias concerns. For example, in speech translation (ST), when translating from languages with notional gender, such as English, into languages where gender-ambiguous terms referring to the speaker are assigned grammatical gender, the speaker's vocal characteristics may play a role in gender assignment. This risks misgendering speakers, whether through masculine defaults or vocal-based assumptions. Yet, how ST models make these decisions remains poorly understood. We investigate the mechanisms ST models use to assign gender to speaker-referring terms across three language pairs (en-es/fr/it), examining how training data patterns, internal language model (ILM) biases, and acoustic information interact. We find that models do not simply replicate term-specific gender associations from training data, but learn broader patterns of masculine prevalence. While the ILM exhibits strong masculine bias, models can override these preferences based on acoustic input. Using contrastive feature attribution on spectrograms, we reveal that the model with higher gender accuracy relies on a previously unknown mechanism: using first-person pronouns to link gendered terms back to the speaker, accessing gender information distributed across the frequency spectrum rather than concentrated in pitch.

papers.title: MarIA and BETO are sexist: evaluating gender bias in large language models for Spanish
papers.research_question: How can gender bias be evaluated in Spanish masked language models, and to what extent is it present in popular pretrained models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an evaluation framework for gender bias in Spanish masked language models and finds varying levels of bias, with body-related adjectives more associated with women and behavior-related adjectives with men.
papers.conclusion: Gender bias is evident in Spanish language models, and the proposed evaluation framework provides interpretable metrics to measure it, which is crucial for deploying fair models in real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias is present in all evaluated Spanish language models.
Bias is most pronounced in body-related adjectives for female templates and behavior-related adjectives for male templates.
The proposed metrics (BPI and BRI) effectively quantify bias across different adjective categorization schemes.
Models like BETO and MarIA show strong bias, while some BERTIN variants are less biased.
The framework is extensible to other protected attributes and languages.
future_direction: Extend evaluation to other biases such as ethnicity, religion, or socio-economic status.
Apply the models to other tasks like text generation or sentiment prediction to study bias propagation.
Research methods to mitigate the identified bias in Spanish models.
papers.abstract: Abstract The study of bias in language models is a growing area of work, however, both research and resources are focused on English. In this paper, we make a first approach focusing on gender bias in some freely available Spanish language models trained using popular deep neural networks, like BERT or RoBERTa. Some of these models are known for achieving state-of-the-art results on downstream tasks. These promising results have promoted such models' integration in many real-world applications and production environments, which could be detrimental to people affected for those systems. This work proposes an evaluation framework to identify gender bias in masked language models, with explainability in mind to ease the interpretation of the evaluation results. We have evaluated 20 different models for Spanish, including some of the most popular pretrained ones in the research community. Our findings state that varying levels of gender bias are present across these models. This approach compares the adjectives proposed by the model for a set of templates. We classify the given adjectives into understandable categories and compute two new metrics from model predictions, one based on the internal state (probability) and the other one on the external state (rank). Those metrics are used to reveal biased models according to the given categories and quantify the degree of bias of the models under study.

papers.title: Large Language Models Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts Across Typologically Diverse Languages
papers.research_question: In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphosyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages.
papers.core_contribution: Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.
papers.conclusion: Large language models share representations of morphosyntactic concepts across typologically diverse languages, suggesting that they develop cross-lingual abstractions, even when trained primarily on English.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of morphosyntactic concepts are shared across languages, with significant overlap in the top features encoding grammatical categories.
Probing classifiers crucially rely on multilingual features to predict morphosyntactic concepts; ablating multilingual features drops performance to near-chance.
Intervening on single multilingual features can change model behavior in machine translation tasks, demonstrating their causal role.
Interventions are selective, primarily affecting the targeted concept without interfering with other concepts.
Sparse autoencoder features are human-interpretable and activate on relevant grammatical concepts across languages.
papers.limitation:
Distinction between model understanding and generation; some features with high causal effect on probes do not necessarily affect generation.
Human biases in feature interpretation; human explanations of features may be biased and suboptimal.
Sparse autoencoders only recover linearly encoded features; non-linearly encoded concepts may not be captured.
papers.abstract: Human bilinguals often use similar brain regions to process multiple languages, depending on when they learned their second language and their proficiency. In large language models (LLMs), how are multiple languages learned and encoded? In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphsyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages. We train sparse autoencoders on Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B, and demonstrate that abstract grammatical concepts are often encoded in feature directions shared across many languages. We use causal interventions to verify the multilingual nature of these representations; specifically, we show that ablating only multilingual features decreases classifier performance to near-chance across languages. We then use these features to precisely modify model behavior in a machine translation task; this demonstrates both the generality and selectivity of these feature's roles in the network. Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.

papers.title: On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages: a Case Study on the Subject-verb Agreement Task
papers.research_question: How universal are the circuits implemented by language models for solving the same task across different languages? Specifically, the paper investigates whether the circuits for subject-verb agreement are similar in English and Spanish.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that the circuits for subject-verb agreement in English and Spanish in Gemma models are highly consistent, driven by an attention head that writes a language-independent subject number signal into the residual stream, which is read by downstream MLP neurons. This direction can causally steer the model's predictions across languages.
papers.conclusion: The circuits for subject-verb agreement are highly consistent across English and Spanish in Gemma models, with a language-independent subject number direction written by an attention head and read by MLP neurons, which can causally steer predictions across languages.
papers.key_findings:
The circuits for subject-verb agreement in English and Spanish are highly consistent in Gemma 2B.
A specific attention head (L13H7 in Gemma 2B) writes a subject number signal as a direction in the residual stream.
Downstream MLP neurons (e.g., neuron 2069 in MLP13) read this signal to promote the correct verb number.
The subject number direction is language-independent; steering with the English direction flips Spanish predictions.
Similar circuits are found in Gemma 7B and Gemma 2 2B, with analogous attention heads (L22H6 and L19H3) playing the same role.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses solely on Gemma models, which may not generalize to other model families.
The study is limited to two languages (English and Spanish), and cannot conclude that the same applies to all other languages, particularly those that are more linguistically distant.
future_direction: Further research could explore whether this pattern holds true for even larger models or across other model families.
papers.abstract: Several algorithms implemented by language models have recently been successfully reversed-engineered. However, these findings have been concentrated on specific tasks and models, leaving it unclear how universal circuits are across different settings. In this paper, we study the circuits implemented by Gemma 2B for solving the subject-verb agreement task across two different languages, English and Spanish. We discover that both circuits are highly consistent, being mainly driven by a particular attention head writing a `subject number' signal to the last residual stream, which is read by a small set of neurons in the final MLPs. Notably, this subject number signal is represented as a direction in the residual stream space, and is language-independent. We demonstrate that this direction has a causal effect on the model predictions, effectively flipping the Spanish predicted verb number by intervening with the direction found in English. Finally, we present evidence of similar behavior in other models within the Gemma 1 and Gemma 2 families.

papers.title: Identifying and Adapting Transformer-Components Responsible for Gender Bias in an English Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we identify transformer components causally responsible for gender bias in language models, and can targeted fine-tuning of these components mitigate bias while preserving general language modeling performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DiffMask+, an efficient method for identifying transformer components causally responsible for gender bias, and demonstrates that targeted fine-tuning of these components can mitigate bias with minimal degradation in general language modeling performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that causal methods can identify components responsible for gender bias, and that parameter-efficient fine-tuning of these components can mitigate bias with minimal harm to language modeling capabilities, though it underscores challenges in defining and measuring bias.
papers.key_findings:
The three causal discovery methods (CMA, ACDC, DiffMask+) identify largely overlapping sets of attention heads, primarily located in the last four layers of GPT-2 small.
Targeted fine-tuning of the identified attention heads reduces gender bias on the CrowS-Pairs and Professions datasets.
Fine-tuning only the identified heads preserves general language modeling performance (perplexity and BLiMP scores) better than full model fine-tuning or fine-tuning broader sets of components.
The dataset used for component discovery influences which components are identified, highlighting the sensitivity of causal methods to dataset choice.
DiffMask+ is computationally more efficient than automated circuit discovery (ACDC) while achieving similar results.
papers.limitation:
Operationalizing gender bias using minimal pairs of contrasting sentences simplifies gender as a binary construct and may not generalize well to other languages.
Causal discovery procedures are sensitive to the choice of dataset, which can affect the components identified.
future_direction: Develop more reliable and validated bias measures.
More attention to dataset development for bias analysis.
Extend mitigation strategies to other types of bias.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) exhibit and amplify many types of undesirable biases learned from the training data, including gender bias. However, we lack tools for effectively and efficiently changing this behavior without hurting general language modeling performance. In this paper, we study three methods for identifying causal relations between LM components and particular output: causal mediation analysis, automated circuit discovery and our novel, efficient method called DiffMask+ based on differential masking. We apply the methods to GPT-2 small and the problem of gender bias, and use the discovered sets of components to perform parameter-efficient fine-tuning for bias mitigation. Our results show significant overlap in the identified components (despite huge differences in the computational requirements of the methods) as well as success in mitigating gender bias, with less damage to general language modeling compared to full model fine-tuning. However, our work also underscores the difficulty of defining and measuring bias, and the sensitivity of causal discovery procedures to dataset choice. We hope our work can contribute to more attention for dataset development, and lead to more effective mitigation strategies for other types of bias.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Gender Bias in LLMs via Interpretable Neuron Editing
papers.research_question: How can we understand the neuron-level mechanisms of gender bias in LLMs and mitigate this bias through targeted neuron editing without compromising the model's core capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretable neuron editing method that effectively reduces gender bias in LLMs while preserving their original capabilities, supported by a new dataset and a detailed analysis of bias mechanisms at the neuron level.
papers.conclusion: The proposed interpretable neuron editing method successfully addresses the challenges of understanding and mitigating gender bias in LLMs, achieving a strong balance between fairness and functionality without compromising the models' original capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias is pervasive across multiple LLMs, as evidenced by non-zero entropy differences and skewed proportions in the CommonWords dataset.
Specific neuron circuits, including 'gender neurons' activated by stereotypical words and 'general neurons' activated by the <start> token, are responsible for gender bias.
Editing even a small number of general neurons can significantly degrade the model's performance on common tasks due to hierarchical neuron interactions.
The proposed interpretable neuron editing method, combining logit-based and causal-based strategies, effectively reduces gender bias (e.g., improving ICAT scores) while maintaining performance on tasks like reading comprehension and arithmetic.
The method outperforms existing fine-tuning and neuron editing approaches in balancing bias reduction with capability preservation.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on the CommonWords dataset for neuron selection, and results may vary for tasks or datasets not covered in the study.
Experiments are conducted on five decoder-only LLMs, requiring potential adaptations for other architectures.
The evaluation metrics (ICAT, entropy difference, accuracy) may not fully capture fairness or real-world performance.
The interpretability insights guiding neuron selection rely on assumptions (e.g., projecting neurons into vocabulary space) that may only be approximations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit gender bias, posing challenges for their safe deployment. Existing methods to mitigate bias lack a comprehensive understanding of its mechanisms or compromise the model's core capabilities. To address these issues, we propose the CommonWords dataset, to systematically evaluate gender bias in LLMs. Our analysis reveals pervasive bias across models and identifies specific neuron circuits, including gender neurons and general neurons, responsible for this behavior. Notably, editing even a small number of general neurons can disrupt the model's overall capabilities due to hierarchical neuron interactions. Based on these insights, we propose an interpretable neuron editing method that combines logit-based and causal-based strategies to selectively target biased neurons. Experiments on five LLMs demonstrate that our method effectively reduces gender bias while preserving the model's original capabilities, outperforming existing fine-tuning and editing approaches. Our findings contribute a novel dataset, a detailed analysis of bias mechanisms, and a practical solution for mitigating gender bias in LLMs.

papers.title: What Triggers my Model? Contrastive Explanations Inform Gender Choices by Translation Models
papers.research_question: How to measure attribution levels of source words on machine translation model's gender decisions, which source words are most salient, and to what extent salient words agree with human perceptions.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how contrastive explanations and saliency attribution can be used to understand gender bias in machine translation models, showing high overlap between model-attributed salient words and human annotations, with differences in part-of-speech categories and dependency distances.
papers.conclusion: The study moves beyond measuring bias to exploring its origins by comparing model and human perceptions, highlighting the importance of understanding model behavior for mitigating gender bias in machine translation.
papers.key_findings:
High overlap between model salient words and human annotations, with the best overlap achieved at the top 15% relative attribution threshold.
Nouns and verbs are the most salient part-of-speech categories for the model's gender decisions.
Salient words for the model are typically at a closer dependency distance to the target referent compared to human annotations.
The model predominantly translates gender-ambiguous referents into masculine forms, while human annotations show more variation.
Different approaches to measuring attribution levels yield varying overlaps, with relative attribution scores performing best.
papers.limitation:
The dataset comprising 60 sentences is very small.
Only one model (OPUS-MT) and two language pairs (EN→DE/ES) were tested.
Model tokenization impacts saliency analysis, and subword merging may introduce errors.
There is low inter-annotator agreement in human annotations, indicating variability in human perceptions.
The study focuses on binary gender, excluding non-binary or inclusive translations.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to a larger dataset once available.
Compare different models and languages in future work.
Address the limitation of available open-source models and toolkits for contrastive approaches.
papers.abstract: Interpretability can be implemented as a means to understand decisions taken by (black box) models, such as machine translation (MT) or large language models (LLMs). Yet, research in this area has been limited in relation to a manifested problem in these models: gender bias. With this research, we aim to move away from simply measuring bias to exploring its origins. Working with gender-ambiguous natural source data, this study examines which context, in the form of input tokens in the source sentence, influences (or triggers) the translation model choice of a certain gender inflection in the target language. To analyse this, we use contrastive explanations and compute saliency attribution. We first address the challenge of a lacking scoring threshold and specifically examine different attribution levels of source words on the model gender decisions in the translation. We compare salient source words with human perceptions of gender and demonstrate a noticeable overlap between human perceptions and model attribution. Additionally, we provide a linguistic analysis of salient words. Our work showcases the relevance of understanding model translation decisions in terms of gender, how this compares to human decisions and that this information should be leveraged to mitigate gender bias.

papers.title: Predicting and Explaining French Grammatical Gender
papers.research_question: How to predict and explain French grammatical gender using interpretable neural models with a global surrogate approach?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces interpretable neural models for French grammatical gender prediction, using a global surrogate approach with auxiliary attributes to provide tunable explanation complexity.
papers.conclusion: Orthography predicts the grammatical gender in French with high accuracy, and adding semantic features can improve this prediction. The black-box embedding can be explained by simpler decision tree models over a given auxiliary explanation space, both locally and globally.
papers.key_findings:
Orthography alone achieves 92.5% accuracy in predicting French grammatical gender.
Adding semantic information improves accuracy to 94.01%.
Phonological features provide less predictive power than orthography in French.
Feminine gender nouns are more explainable than masculine nouns due to more specific rules.
Global explanations lead to fewer overall rules but are more complex per instance, while local explanations are more accurate but may have inconsistent rules.
papers.limitation: Local explanations may lead to inconsistent rules for distant test points, which can be undesirable in applications like language learning.
future_direction: Cross-linguistic extension of the study
Human-in-the-loop curation for identifying new auxiliary attributes
papers.abstract: Grammatical gender may be determined by semantics, orthography, phonology, or could even be arbitrary. Identifying patterns in the factors that govern noun genders can be useful for language learners, and for understanding innate linguistic sources of gender bias. Traditional manual rule-based approaches may be substituted by more accurate and scalable but harder-to-interpret computational approaches for predicting gender from typological information. In this work, we propose interpretable gender classification models for French, which obtain the best of both worlds. We present high accuracy neural approaches which are augmented by a novel global surrogate based approach for explaining predictions. We introduce auxiliary attributes to provide tunable explanation complexity.

papers.title: Same Neurons, Different Languages: Probing Morphosyntax in Multilingual Pre-trained Models
papers.research_question: Does multilingual pre-trained models encode morphosyntactic information in the same subset of neurons across different languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual pre-trained models develop cross-lingually entangled representations of morphosyntax, with neuron overlap varying by category and influenced by language proximity and pre-training data size.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual pre-trained models implicitly align morphosyntactic information across languages by using overlapping subsets of neurons, which may affect their cross-lingual transfer capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Significant cross-lingual overlap exists in neurons encoding morphosyntactic information.
Overlap varies across morphosyntactic categories and is lower for categories with larger inventories of possible values.
Overlap is higher for languages within the same genus or with similar typological features.
Overlap increases with pre-training data size but decreases with larger model size (comparing XLM-R-base and XLM-R-large).
XLM-R-base tends to share more neurons than m-BERT for encoding morphosyntactic attributes.
future_direction: Artificially encouraging neuron overlap to facilitate zero-shot cross-lingual inference to low-resource and typologically distant languages.
papers.abstract: The success of multilingual pre-trained models is underpinned by their ability to learn representations shared by multiple languages even in absence of any explicit supervision. However, it remains unclear how these models learn to generalise across languages. In this work, we conjecture that multilingual pre-trained models can derive language-universal abstractions about grammar. In particular, we investigate whether morphosyntactic information is encoded in the same subset of neurons in different languages. We conduct the first large-scale empirical study over 43 languages and 14 morphosyntactic categories with a state-of-the-art neuron-level probe. Our findings show that the cross-lingual overlap between neurons is significant, but its extent may vary across categories and depends on language proximity and pre-training data size.

papers.title: The Geometry of Multilingual Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models maintain a shared multilingual representation space while still encoding language-sensitive information in each language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, facilitating feature extraction for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual language models encode features along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, enabling targeted extraction of features for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
Languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, as shown by causal effects on language modeling performance and direct subspace comparisons.
Subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that encode information such as token vocabularies, and shifting representations by language means is sufficient to induce token predictions in different languages.
Stable language-neutral axes encode information such as token positions and part-of-speech, and these axes are orthogonal to language-sensitive axes.
The identified axes (both language-sensitive and language-neutral) are relatively stable across middle layers of the model.
Token position information is encoded along nonlinear structures like spirals, toruses, and curves in the representation space.
future_direction: Investigate how nonlinear structures (e.g., spirals, toruses) arise from and interact with the dot product self-attention mechanism in Transformer models.
Conduct a more detailed analysis of how specific representational structures are retained across layers.

Assess how multilingual language models encode more complex linguistic features geometrically, and the extent to which representation spaces can be fully decomposed into orthogonal subspaces encoding different features.
papers.abstract: We assess how multilingual language models maintain a shared multilingual representation space while still encoding language-sensitive information in each language. Using XLM-R as a case study, we show that languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, evaluated based on causal effects on language modeling performance and direct comparisons between subspaces for 88 languages. The subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that are relatively stable throughout middle layers, and these axes encode information such as token vocabularies. Shifting representations by language means is sufficient to induce token predictions in different languages. However, we also identify stable language-neutral axes that encode information such as token positions and part-of-speech. We visualize representations projected onto language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, identifying language family and part-of-speech clusters, along with spirals, toruses, and curves representing token position information. These results demonstrate that multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, allowing the models to extract a variety of features for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.

papers.title: Unsupervised Concept Vector Extraction for Bias Control in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we extract concept representations (like gender) from LLMs without labeled data and use them to measure and manipulate bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method (WMD) for extracting concept steering vectors from LLMs and a projection-based intervention method for bias mitigation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method is effective for extracting steering vectors and mitigating bias in LLMs, and it generalizes to other protected attributes like race.
papers.key_findings:
The WMD method extracts steering vectors that have higher correlation with gender bias than the difference-in-means method.
The projection-based intervention effectively reduces gender bias in model predictions.
The method generalizes to racial bias.
Steering vectors can be transferred to different tasks (Winogenerated and occupational stereotypes).
Debiasing via steering does not significantly harm general model capabilities (MMLU and IFEVAL).
papers.limitation:
The approach oversimplifies gender as a binary concept and does not account for non-binary identities.
The method may not be applicable when factual gender information is needed in predictions.
future_direction: Expand evaluation to a broader range of tasks.
Adopt a more comprehensive approach that considers intersectionality of gender with other social identities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are known to perpetuate stereotypes and exhibit biases. Various strategies have been proposed to mitigate these biases, but most work studies biases as a black-box problem without considering how concepts are represented within the model. We adapt techniques from representation engineering to study how the concept of "gender" is represented within LLMs. We introduce a new method that extracts concept representations via probability weighting without labeled data and efficiently selects a steering vector for measuring and manipulating the model's representation. We develop a projection-based method that enables precise steering of model predictions and demonstrate its effectiveness in mitigating gender bias in LLMs and show that it also generalizes to racial bias. Our code is available at: https://github.com/hannahxchen/gender-bias-steering
