papers.title: Cross-Lingual Generalization and Compression: From Language-Specific to Shared Neurons
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models achieve cross-lingual generalization?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides empirical evidence that cross-lingual generalization in multilingual language models emerges through compression during pre-training, with representations evolving from language-specific to shared cross-lingual abstractions, demonstrated via neuron analysis and manipulation.
papers.conclusion: Cross-lingual generalization in multilingual language models emerges through compression during pre-training, leading to the development of shared concept neurons across languages that encode generalized semantic representations.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual models initially form language-specific representations which gradually converge into cross-lingual abstractions as training progresses.
Language identification probing reveals a shift from uniform capabilities across layers to specialized layer functions, with middle layers becoming more language-agnostic.
Specific neurons emerge as reliable predictors for the same semantic concepts across different languages, showing increasing alignment during training.
Neuron manipulation experiments demonstrate that concept-specific neurons identified from one language can guide semantically coherent text generation in another language once cross-lingual generalization is achieved.
The model's internal representations encode shared conceptual knowledge independent of the original language encoding.
papers.limitation: The number of publicly available training checkpoints for the BLOOM models is limited, restricting the granularity of analysis.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities to transfer knowledge across languages, despite being trained without explicit cross-lingual supervision.We analyze the parameter spaces of three MLLMs to study how their representations evolve during pre-training, observing patterns consistent with compression: models initially form language-specific representations, which gradually converge into cross-lingual abstractions as training progresses.Through probing experiments, we observe a clear transition from uniform language identification capabilities across layers to more specialized layer functions.For deeper analysis, we focus on neurons that encode distinct semantic concepts.By tracing their development during pre-training, we show how they gradually align across languages.Notably, we identify specific neurons that emerge as increasingly reliable predictors for the same concepts across languages.This alignment manifests concretely in generation: once an MLLM exhibits cross-lingual generalization according to our measures, we can select concept-specific neurons identified from, e.g., Spanish text and manipulate them to guide token predictions.Remarkably, rather than generating Spanish text, the model produces semantically coherent English text.This demonstrates that cross-lingually aligned neurons encode generalized semantic representations, independent of the original language encoding.

papers.title: Shapley Head Pruning: Identifying and Removing Interference in Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Can we reduce interference in multilingual transformers by identifying and pruning language-specific attention heads, thereby improving performance without adding parameters?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Shapley Head Pruning, a method that uses Shapley Values to identify and remove language-specific attention heads that cause interference in multilingual transformers, thereby improving cross-lingual performance without parameter updates.
papers.conclusion: The method effectively identifies language-specific components and improves cross-lingual performance through pruning, and suggests future work on linguistic features and pre-training.
papers.key_findings:
Attention Head Shapley Values vary across languages, indicating language-specific and language-agnostic heads.
Pruning heads with negative Shapley Values improves performance on XNLI and UDPOS without updating parameters.
The method outperforms random pruning and gradient-based pruning baselines.
Some attention heads show clear language-agnostic patterns (e.g., synonym linking), while others are language-specific.
Zero-shot pruning using English Shapley Values also improves performance for many languages.
papers.limitation:
Computational cost of Shapley Values is high compared to gradient-based methods.
Reliance on attention visualization, which is debated as a sound analytical tool.
future_direction: Exploring the relationship between linguistic features, training data volume, and the language-specificity of attention heads.
Reducing cross-lingual interference introduced by language-specific components during pre-training, such as pruning during pre-training or utilizing sparsely activated networks.
papers.abstract: Multilingual transformer-based models demonstrate remarkable zero and few-shot transfer across languages by learning and reusing language-agnostic features. However, as a fixed-size model acquires more languages, its performance across all languages degrades. Those who attribute this interference phenomenon to limited model capacity address the problem by adding additional parameters, despite evidence that transformer-based models are overparameterized. In this work, we show that it is possible to reduce interference by instead identifying and pruning language-specific attention heads. First, we use Shapley Values, a credit allocation metric from coalitional game theory, to identify attention heads that introduce interference. Then, we show that pruning such heads from a fixed model improves performance for a target language on both sentence classification and structural prediction. Finally, we provide insights on language-agnostic and language-specific attention heads using attention visualization.

papers.title: Discovering Language-neutral Sub-networks in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent do multilingual pre-trained language models learn language-neutral representations, and what is the effect of such representations on cross-lingual transfer performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual language models contain language-neutral sub-networks that are topologically similar across languages and can be effectively transferred for cross-lingual tasks, but this transferability decreases at higher sparsity levels.
papers.conclusion: The results suggest that multilingual language models include separate language-neutral and language-specific components, with the language-neutral components playing a more prominent role in cross-lingual transfer performance.
papers.key_findings:
Winning tickets (sub-networks) can be found for each language and task at multiple sparsity levels, though performance degrades at higher sparsity.
Sub-networks for different languages have high parameter overlap, especially for NER and XNLI tasks, indicating language-neutral components.
Cross-lingual transfer of winning tickets is effective for XNLI and NER, but less so for MLM, and transfer performance degrades at higher sparsity.
The language-neutral components are more prominent in the middle to upper layers of the model.
Combining multiple languages during pruning can yield sub-networks that transfer better to low-resource languages.
papers.limitation:
Parameter overlap may not be a fine-grained measure for identifying language-neutral components, as small differences in cross-lingual performance do not strongly correlate with overlap.
Only the lottery ticket hypothesis is used for discovering sub-networks, while other pruning and masking methods may provide complementary or competing insights.
Due to computational limitations, the analysis is limited to three tasks and eleven languages, and new insights may emerge from a larger cross-section.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pre-trained language models transfer remarkably well on cross-lingual downstream tasks. However, the extent to which they learn language-neutral representations (i.e., shared representations that encode similar phenomena across languages), and the effect of such representations on cross-lingual transfer performance, remain open questions. In this work, we conceptualize language neutrality of multilingual models as a function of the overlap between language-encoding subnetworks of these models. We employ the lottery ticket hypothesis to discover sub-networks that are individually optimized for various languages and tasks. Our evaluation across three distinct tasks and eleven typologically-diverse languages demonstrates that sub-networks for different languages are topologically similar (i.e., language-neutral), making them effective initializations for cross-lingual transfer with limited performance degradation. 1

papers.title: Different Speech Translation Models Encode and Translate Speaker Gender Differently
papers.research_question: Does gender encoding found in speech models also hold for speech translation (ST) models? If so, what are the implications for the speaker’s gender assignment in translation?
papers.core_contribution: Traditional encoder-decoder speech translation models capture speaker gender information, while newer speech+MT architectures (with adapters) do not. Low gender encoding capabilities result in a tendency toward masculine default translations, a bias more pronounced in newer architectures.
papers.conclusion: ST models can leverage acoustic gender information when available. When such information is weakly encoded, the models default to masculine translations more frequently.
papers.key_findings:
Traditional encoder-decoder ST models encode speaker gender information, while newer speech+MT models (with adapters) do not.
Gender encoding capability correlates with gender translation accuracy: higher encoding leads to more accurate gender translation.
When gender encoding is low, models default to masculine translations.
Adapters in speech+MT models remove gender information.
Gender information is primarily encoded in the early positions of the sequence.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to specific models and language directions.
Probing does not directly confirm whether the model uses the extracted information.
future_direction: Explore which properties of adapters contribute to the loss of gender information.
Expand analysis to additional translation systems and languages, and systems integrating speech into LLMs.
Explore further interpretability techniques, such as amnesic probing or mechanistic interpretability.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on interpreting the hidden states of speech models have shown their ability to capture speaker-specific features, including gender. Does this finding also hold for speech translation (ST) models? If so, what are the implications for the speaker's gender assignment in translation? We address these questions from an interpretability perspective, using probing methods to assess gender encoding across diverse ST models. Results on three language directions (English-French/Italian/Spanish) indicate that while traditional encoder-decoder models capture gender information, newer architectures -- integrating a speech encoder with a machine translation system via adapters -- do not. We also demonstrate that low gender encoding capabilities result in systems' tendency toward a masculine default, a translation bias that is more pronounced in newer architectures.

papers.title: How Language Models Prioritize Contextual Grammatical Cues?
papers.research_question: How do language models handle gender agreement when multiple valid gender cue words are present in the context, and which contextual cues do they prioritize?
papers.core_contribution: Encoder-based models (BERT) tend to prioritize the first cue in the context for gender agreement, while decoder-based models (GPT-2) rely more on the final cue.
papers.conclusion: Encoder-based and decoder-based Transformer language models behave differently in prioritizing contextual cues for gender agreement, with BERT relying on earlier cues and GPT-2 on later ones.
papers.key_findings:
BERT significantly incorporates earlier cue words into the representation of the target word, starting from the middle layers.
GPT-2 significantly attends to the later cue words in the context, starting from earlier layers and peaking near the final layer.
The predictions from context-mixing analysis and activation patching are consistent, indicating cues that contribute more to the target representation also play a crucial role in the final decision.
Fine-tuning intensifies the observed behaviors: BERT pays dominantly to the first cue, and GPT-2 increases the importance of the last cue.
The reliance on cue position is consistent even when the first cue is a pronoun instead of a name.
papers.limitation:
Experiments and findings are based on a grammatical agreement task as a well-defined scenario where multiple cues exist in a context.
Experiments were run on two widely used language models but with base size due to limited computational budget.
future_direction: Extend experiments to include more recent, large language models.
Explore other case studies, such as Question Answering datasets, where multiple cues in the context refer to the answer.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models have shown an excellent ability to effectively capture and utilize contextual information. Although various analysis techniques have been used to quantify and trace the contribution of single contextual cues to a target task such as subject-verb agreement or coreference resolution, scenarios in which multiple relevant cues are available in the context remain underexplored. In this paper, we investigate how language models handle gender agreement when multiple gender cue words are present, each capable of independently disambiguating a target gender pronoun. We analyze two widely used Transformer-based models: BERT, an encoder-based, and GPT-2, a decoder-based model. Our analysis employs two complementary approaches: context mixing analysis, which tracks information flow within the model, and a variant of activation patching, which measures the impact of cues on the model's prediction. We find that BERT tends to prioritize the first cue in the context to form both the target word representations and the model's prediction, while GPT-2 relies more on the final cue. Our findings reveal striking differences in how encoder-based and decoder-based models prioritize and use contextual information for their predictions.

papers.title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-Based Localization
papers.research_question: How can we produce visual explanations for decisions from a large class of CNN-based models to make them more transparent and explainable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Grad-CAM, a technique that uses gradients flowing into the final convolutional layer to produce coarse localization maps highlighting important image regions for a prediction, applicable to a wide variety of CNN model families without architectural changes or re-training.
papers.conclusion: Grad-CAM is an effective visualization technique for understanding CNN decisions, providing insights into model behavior, failure modes, and biases, and has been successfully applied to image classification, captioning, and VQA tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Grad-CAM produces class-discriminative localization maps that generalize the earlier CAM approach to a broader range of CNN architectures.
Grad-CAM visualizations help diagnose model failure modes, showing that seemingly unreasonable predictions have reasonable explanations.
Grad-CAM is robust to adversarial perturbations and can identify dataset biases, aiding in model generalization and fairness.
Human studies show that Grad-CAM explanations help users establish appropriate trust in predictions and discern a stronger network from a weaker one.
Grad-CAM can be combined with fine-grained visualizations (Guided Backpropagation) to create Guided Grad-CAM, which is both high-resolution and class-discriminative.
papers.limitation:
Grad-CAM produces coarse, low-resolution heatmaps (e.g., 14x14 for VGG/AlexNet).
The discriminative ability of Grad-CAM reduces when applied to earlier convolutional layers or at downsampling layers in architectures like ResNet.

papers.title: Bias A-head? Analyzing Bias in Transformer-Based Language Model Attention Heads
papers.research_question: How does bias manifest and behave internally in a language model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a framework to identify biased attention heads in transformer-based language models and shows that biases are encoded in a small set of heads, which can be targeted for debiasing.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that biases in language models are encoded in a small set of attention heads, and the proposed framework helps understand and mitigate these biases, contributing to more transparent and fair NLP systems.
papers.key_findings:
Biased attention heads can be identified via gradient-based bias scores, and counter-stereotype experiments validate that these heads encode stereotypes.
The distribution of biased heads differs across models, with GPT-2 having fewer biased heads than BERT.
Masking out a small set of biased heads can reduce model bias with minimal impact on language modeling and NLU performance.
LLaMA-2-Chat exhibits less bias than LLaMA-2, suggesting that RLHF reduces stereotyping.
Prior debiasing strategies may cover up bias rather than remove it, as some anti-bias heads are turned into biased heads after debiasing.
papers.limitation:
Focuses only on stereotyping bias (representational harm) and not allocational bias.
Relies on existing word lists which may have limited coverage for other protected groups and non-English languages.
Focuses on attention heads only, while bias may also manifest in other model components.
Does not investigate heads with negative bias scores (anti-bias heads) in detail.
future_direction: Apply the method to assess biases in larger foundation models like GPT-3 and LLaMA.
Study allocational bias in downstream NLP tasks.
Investigate other model components and anti-bias heads for a more comprehensive understanding.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based pretrained large language models (PLM) such as BERT and GPT have achieved remarkable success in NLP tasks. However, PLMs are prone to encoding stereotypical biases. Although a burgeoning literature has emerged on stereotypical bias mitigation in PLMs, such as work on debiasing gender and racial stereotyping, how such biases manifest and behave internally within PLMs remains largely unknown. Understanding the internal stereotyping mechanisms may allow better assessment of model fairness and guide the development of effective mitigation strategies. In this work, we focus on attention heads, a major component of the Transformer architecture, and propose a bias analysis framework to explore and identify a small set of biased heads that are found to contribute to a PLM's stereotypical bias. We conduct extensive experiments to validate the existence of these biased heads and to better understand how they behave. We investigate gender and racial bias in the English language in two types of Transformer-based PLMs: the encoder-based BERT model and the decoder-based autoregressive GPT model. Overall, the results shed light on understanding the bias behavior in pretrained language models.

papers.title: The Same But Different: Structural Similarities and Differences in Multilingual Language Modeling
papers.research_question: When two languages employ the same morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using shared internal circuitry? When two languages require different morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using different internal circuitry?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs use shared internal circuitry for similar syntactic processes across languages, even in independently trained monolingual models, and employ language-specific components (e.g., feed-forward networks) for language-specific morphological processes.
papers.conclusion: The paper finds that cross-lingual structural similarity is represented within LLMs using shared circuits that invoke the same algorithm independent of language, and that language-specific processing is localized to play a causal role only in languages that require it.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual models use a single circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs.
Monolingual models trained independently on English and Chinese each adopt nearly the same circuit for the IOI task, suggesting consistency in how LLMs learn to handle this aspect of language modeling.
For tasks requiring language-specific morphological processes (e.g., past tense marking in English), multilingual models invoke a largely overlapping circuit but employ language-specific components as needed, such as feed-forward networks in English only for morphological marking.
The circuits identified for the IOI task align with prior work, indicating that the same mechanism is shared between English and Chinese within a multilingual model.
Heads specifically responsible for past tense disambiguation are activated in English but not in Chinese, and they suppress present-tense verbs in English.
papers.limitation: Results are limited to specific tasks and datasets, requiring future work for replication and generalization.
future_direction: Replicate and generalize findings to more tasks and datasets.
Explore cross-disciplinary collaborations to gain fresh perspectives on linguistic universality using LLMs.
Investigate whether circuit overlap can be exploited for improving cross-lingual transfer and safety.
papers.abstract: We employ new tools from mechanistic interpretability in order to ask whether the internal structure of large language models (LLMs) shows correspondence to the linguistic structures which underlie the languages on which they are trained. In particular, we ask (1) when two languages employ the same morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using shared internal circuitry? and (2) when two languages require different morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using different internal circuitry? Using English and Chinese multilingual and monolingual models, we analyze the internal circuitry involved in two tasks. We find evidence that models employ the same circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs, and that this is the case even for monolingual models trained completely independently. Moreover, we show that multilingual models employ language-specific components (attention heads and feed-forward networks) when needed to handle linguistic processes (e.g., morphological marking) that only exist in some languages. Together, our results provide new insights into how LLMs trade off between exploiting common structures and preserving linguistic differences when tasked with modeling multiple languages simultaneously.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: What Language(s) Does Aya-23 Think In? How Multilinguality Affects Internal Language Representations
papers.research_question: How does balanced multilingual training affect internal language processing in LLMs, specifically in terms of language activation, neuron sharing, and layer-wise distribution of language-specific neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Balanced multilingual training leads to distinct internal language processing, with language-specific neurons concentrated in final layers and activation of typologically related languages during translation, unlike English-centric models.
papers.conclusion: Balanced multilingual training fundamentally alters how decoder-only LLMs process language internally, leading to language-specific neurons concentrated in final layers and activation of multiple languages during translation.
papers.key_findings:
Aya-23 activates typologically related language representations during translation, unlike English-centric models that rely on a single pivot language.
Code-mixed neuron activation patterns vary with mixing rates and are shaped more by the base language than the mixed-in one.
Aya-23’s language-specific neurons for code-mixed inputs concentrate in final layers, diverging from prior findings on decoder-only models.
Neuron overlap analysis shows that script similarity and typological relations impact processing across model types.
French-based code-mixed inputs show higher neuron clustering than Chinese-based inputs across all models, regardless of training data composition.
papers.limitation:
Token overlap between languages in the logit lens experiments may affect analysis of language-specific activation patterns.
Neuron specialization analysis using binary activations results in information loss that may obscure subtle activation patterns.
Code-mixed dataset created via rule-based word-to-word translation produces unnatural sentences that may not represent authentic code-switching.
Analysis is limited to three models and may not generalize to other architectures or sizes.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at multilingual tasks, yet their internal language processing remains poorly understood. We analyze how Aya-23-8B, a decoder-only LLM trained on balanced multilingual data, handles code-mixed, cloze, and translation tasks compared to predominantly monolingual models like Llama 3 and Chinese-LLaMA-2. Using logit lens and neuron specialization analyses, we find: (1) Aya-23 activates typologically related language representations during translation, unlike English-centric models that rely on a single pivot language; (2) code-mixed neuron activation patterns vary with mixing rates and are shaped more by the base language than the mixed-in one; and (3) Aya-23's languagespecific neurons for code-mixed inputs concentrate in final layers, diverging from prior findings on decoder-only models. Neuron overlap analysis further shows that script similarity and typological relations impact processing across model types. These findings reveal how multilingual training shapes LLM internals and inform future cross-lingual transfer research.

papers.title: A Tale of Pronouns: Interpretability Informs Gender Bias Mitigation for Fairer Instruction-Tuned Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Whether and to what extent instruction-tuned models exhibit gender bias in machine translation and how interpretability can inform bias mitigation.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses interpretability (word attribution scores) to understand gender bias in instruction-tuned machine translation models and proposes a simple few-shot debiasing method guided by these scores.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability is a valuable tool for both diagnosing and mitigating gender bias in instruction-tuned language models for machine translation.
papers.key_findings:
Instruction-tuned models default to male-inflected translations, even when female pronouns are present.
Interpretability analysis reveals that models systematically overlook the gender-marking pronoun in misgendered translations.
A few-shot debiasing approach, using interpretability scores to select exemplars, leads to significantly fairer translations with only four human-written examples.
Flan-T5 generally outperforms mT0 in translation accuracy and fairness metrics.
The proposed debiasing method improves accuracy and reduces bias metrics (∆G and ∆S) for Spanish translations.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to two target languages (German and Spanish).
The analysis uses a template-based dataset (WinoMT), which simplifies the sentence structure.
Few-shot experiments are conducted only with the largest model variants due to translation quality and computational constraints.
future_direction: Expanding the study to more languages.
Extending the methodology to natural machine translation setups.
papers.abstract: Recent instruction fine-tuned models can solve multiple NLP tasks when prompted to do so, with machine translation (MT) being a prominent use case. However, current research often focuses on standard performance benchmarks, leaving compelling fairness and ethical considerations behind. In MT, this might lead to misgendered translations, resulting, among other harms, in the perpetuation of stereotypes and prejudices. In this work, we address this gap by investigating whether and to what extent such models exhibit gender bias in machine translation and how we can mitigate it. Concretely, we compute established gender bias metrics on the WinoMT corpus from English to German and Spanish. We discover that IFT models default to male-inflected translations, even disregarding female occupational stereotypes. Next, using interpretability methods, we unveil that models systematically overlook the pronoun indicating the gender of a target occupation in misgendered translations. Finally, based on this finding, we propose an easy-to-implement and effective bias mitigation solution based on few-shot learning that leads to significantly fairer translations.

papers.title: How Gender Debiasing Affects Internal Model Representations, and Why It Matters
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between extrinsic and intrinsic gender bias in NLP models? How does debiasing affect internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework using information-theoretic probing (compression) as an intrinsic bias metric, showing it is a better indicator of debiasing than CEAT and can expose superficial debiasing where extrinsic metrics improve but internal representations remain biased.
papers.conclusion: The compression rate (gender extractability) is a useful intrinsic indicator for gender bias in NLP models, providing confidence in debiasing efforts and helping detect superficial debiasing before deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Gender extractability measured by compression is a more reliable indicator of gender bias in NLP models than the CEAT metric.
High gender extractability with low extrinsic bias indicates superficial debiasing, where bias remains in internal representations and can be restored by retraining the classification layer.
The correlation between intrinsic (compression) and extrinsic bias metrics varies by task, but compression shows higher correlations than CEAT.
Different debiasing strategies (scrubbing, balancing, anonymization, counterfactual augmentation) have varying effects on intrinsic and extrinsic bias.
The classification layer plays a significant role in bias, and debiasing must address both the language model's internal representations and the classifier.
papers.limitation: The study uses gender as a binary variable, which is trans-exclusive.
future_direction: Adjust the framework to non-binary genders.
papers.abstract: Common studies of gender bias in NLP focus either on extrinsic bias measured by model performance on a downstream task or on intrinsic bias found in models' internal representations. However, the relationship between extrinsic and intrinsic bias is relatively unknown. In this work, we illuminate this relationship by measuring both quantities together: we debias a model during downstream fine-tuning, which reduces extrinsic bias, and measure the effect on intrinsic bias, which is operationalized as bias extractability with information-theoretic probing. Through experiments on two tasks and multiple bias metrics, we show that our intrinsic bias metric is a better indicator of debiasing than (a contextual adaptation of) the standard WEAT metric, and can also expose cases of superficial debiasing. Our framework provides a comprehensive perspective on bias in NLP models, which can be applied to deploy NLP systems in a more informed manner. Our code and model checkpoints are publicly available.

papers.title: On the Mutual Influence of Gender and Occupation in LLM Representations
papers.research_question: How do occupations and the gender perception of first names mutually influence each other in LLM representations, and how do internal gender representations relate to biased behavior in downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes the mutual influence between gender and occupation representations in LLMs, showing that first-name gender representations correlate with real-world statistics and shift with occupational context, and that these internal representations partially explain biased behavior in downstream occupation prediction, though with noisy correlation.
papers.conclusion: The gender representation of first names interacts with stereotypical occupations in context, sometimes revealing model bias in downstream tasks, but the noisy correlation between internal gender representations and extrinsic biased behavior underscores the need for more robust bias detection methods.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs' internal gender representations of first names correlate with real-world gender distributions associated with those names.
The gender representation of a first name in LLMs is influenced by the occupational context, shifting towards femininity with female-dominated occupations and masculinity with male-dominated occupations.
In a downstream occupation prediction task, LLMs achieve higher true positive rates when the perceived gender of a first name aligns with the gender stereotype of the occupation.
There is a moderate correlation between internal gender representations (dot product with gender direction) and extrinsic biased behavior, but this correlation is noisy and not reliable for bias detection.
The first principal component of gendered word embedding differences effectively approximates the gender direction in LLMs, as validated by binary gender classification accuracy.
papers.limitation:
Underrepresentation of gender identities beyond the binary female-male definition in the gender direction approximation.
Limited coverage of demographic identities, with first names only from two genders and four races/ethnicities within the U.S. context.
Under-exploration of model size effects due to resource constraints, using only four LLMs of similar sizes.
future_direction: Inclusion of additional gender identities in embedding analysis.
Collecting first names that represent other genders, races, and ethnicities for a more comprehensive study.
Exploring how model size affects gender representation and bias.
papers.abstract: We examine LLM representations of gender for first names in various occupational contexts to study how occupations and the gender perception of first names in LLMs influence each other mutually. We find that LLMs' first-name gender representations correlate with real-world gender statistics associated with the name, and are influenced by the co-occurrence of stereotypically feminine or masculine occupations. Additionally, we study the influence of first-name gender representations on LLMs in a downstream occupation prediction task and their potential as an internal metric to identify extrinsic model biases. While feminine first-name embeddings often raise the probabilities for female-dominated jobs (and vice versa for male-dominated jobs), reliably using these internal gender representations for bias detection remains challenging.

papers.title: A Joint Matrix Factorization Analysis of Multilingual Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models encode morphosyntactic features in their layers? Are the findings robust in low-resource settings? How do morphosyntactic typology and downstream task performance relate to the factorization outputs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a joint matrix factorization analysis tool for comparing multilingual and monolingual representations, and uses it to study morphosyntactic feature encoding across 33 languages and 17 categories, finding variations across layers and language properties.
papers.conclusion: The introduced tool provides insights into language representation in multilingual models and has practical implications for improving performance in cross-lingual tasks. Future work will extend the analysis to multimodal models.
papers.key_findings:
Encoding of morphosyntactic information varies across upper and lower layers, with category-specific differences influenced by language properties such as writing system and number of unique characters.
Logographic writing systems (Chinese, Japanese) lead to distinct representations and present unique challenges for multilingual models.
Multilingual representations show distinct encoding patterns in subsets of languages with low language proximity.
Representation of low-resource languages benefits from the presence of related languages.
Factorization outputs yield a phylogenetic tree structure similar to linguists' trees and correlate with cross-lingual task performance.
papers.limitation:
Only used RoBERTa and XLM-R, not other models like BERT, mBERT, T5, mT5 due to computational resources.
Downsampled Wikipedia to 200MB per language, though validated with a public XLM-R checkpoint.
Analyses limited to morphosyntactic features, plan to expand to semantics and pragmatics.
future_direction: Extend the analysis tool to examine representations learned by multimodal models.
Expand the analysis to other linguistic aspects, such as semantics and pragmatics.
papers.abstract: We present an analysis tool based on joint matrix factorization for comparing latent representations of multilingual and monolingual models. An alternative to probing, this tool allows us to analyze multiple sets of representations in a joint manner. Using this tool, we study to what extent and how morphosyntactic features are reflected in the representations learned by multilingual pre-trained models. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of over 33 languages and 17 morphosyntactic categories. Our findings demonstrate variations in the encoding of morphosyntactic information across upper and lower layers, with category-specific differences influenced by language properties. Hierarchical clustering of the factorization outputs yields a tree structure that is related to phylogenetic trees manually crafted by linguists. Moreover, we find the factorization outputs exhibit strong associations with performance observed across different cross-lingual tasks. We release our code to facilitate future research.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual Activation Steering for Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: How can inference-time neuron activation steering improve cross-lingual transfer in multilingual language models without additional training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-Lingual Activation Steering (CLAS), a training-free inference-time method that modulates neuron activations to improve cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LLMs by rebalancing shared and language-specific representations.
papers.conclusion: CLAS effectively improves cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LLMs by steering activations to promote functional divergence, with gains not reliant on geometric alignment to the anchor language.
papers.key_findings:
CLAS achieves average improvements of 2.3% (Acc.) and 3.4% (F1) on classification and generation benchmarks, respectively.
Performance improvements are driven by functional divergence, with gains correlating with increased language cluster separation rather than closer alignment to English.
CLAS reduces cosine similarity to English for non-anchor languages, indicating a shift away from strict geometric alignment.
Qualitative analysis shows CLAS suppresses repetition loops and verbosity in generation outputs.
The steering parameter alpha can be positive or negative for optimal performance, indicating task- and model-dependent balance between shared and language-specific signals.
papers.limitation:
Analysis and intervention are anchored to English, which may not generalize to other anchor languages.
CLAS is not uniformly beneficial and can cause performance regressions for some languages.
Mechanistic analysis does not isolate attention heads or other circuit components, limiting causal attribution.
future_direction: Explore adaptive steering strategies based on representational structure.
Better understand saturation effects in well-separated language clusters.
Extend CLAS to other modalities and training settings.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit strong multilingual capabilities, yet significant performance gaps persist between dominant and non-dominant languages. Prior work attributes this gap to imbalances between shared and language-specific neurons in multilingual representations. We propose Cross-Lingual Activation Steering (CLAS), a training-free inference-time intervention that selectively modulates neuron activations. We evaluate CLAS on classification and generation benchmarks, achieving average improvements of 2.3% (Acc.) and 3.4% (F1) respectively, while maintaining high-resource language performance. We discover that effective transfer operates through functional divergence rather than strict alignment; performance gains correlate with increased language cluster separation. Our results demonstrate that targeted activation steering can unlock latent multilingual capacity in existing models without modification to model weights.

papers.title: Investigating Bias Representations in Llama 2 Chat via Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How does activation steering reveal and mitigate societal biases in Llama 2 7B Chat, and what does this say about the model's internal representations of bias?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering uncovers inherent gender bias in Llama 2 7B Chat and shows that RLHF leads to increased similarity in the model's representation of different societal biases, suggesting a loss of nuanced understanding.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering is effective for red-teaming biases in LLMs, and RLHF may cause the model to conflate different bias types, reducing nuanced understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Llama 2 7B Chat exhibits inherent gender bias despite undergoing Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF).
Bias steering vectors trigger refusal responses, and subtracting a refusal vector can elicit biased outputs from the model.
Bias vectors are transferable across dimensions; for example, racial bias steering can elicit gender and religion bias.
There is a negative correlation between bias vectors and refusal vectors, as shown by cosine similarity across layers.
RLHF increases the cosine similarity between different bias vectors in the Chat model compared to the base model, indicating that biases become more closely associated.
papers.abstract: We address the challenge of societal bias in Large Language Models (LLMs), focusing on the Llama 2 7B Chat model. As LLMs are increasingly integrated into decision-making processes with substantial societal impact, it becomes imperative to ensure these models do not reinforce existing biases. Our approach employs activation steering to probe for and mitigate biases related to gender, race, and religion. This method manipulates model activations to direct responses towards or away from biased outputs, utilizing steering vectors derived from the StereoSet dataset and custom GPT4 generated gender bias prompts. Our findings reveal inherent gender bias in Llama 2 7B Chat, persisting even after Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). We also observe a predictable negative correlation between bias and the model's tendency to refuse responses. Significantly, our study uncovers that RLHF tends to increase the similarity in the model's representation of different forms of societal biases, which raises questions about the model's nuanced understanding of different forms of bias. This work also provides valuable insights into effective red-teaming strategies for LLMs using activation steering, particularly emphasizing the importance of integrating a refusal vector.

papers.title: Why do LLaVA Vision-Language Models Reply to Images in English?
papers.research_question: Why do LLaVA-style vision-language models tend to reply in English when an image is included in the query, regardless of the query language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes Image-induced Fidelity Loss (IFL) in LLaVA models, finding the bias originates in the language backbone and can be mitigated by using bilingual language models or through a mechanistic intervention on intermediate attention layers.
papers.conclusion: Image-induced Fidelity Loss is a significant issue in LLaVA models, localized within the language model component. Improving the multilinguality of the underlying LLM is a promising path for building more robust multilingual VLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Adding an image to a query significantly reduces the probability of a LLaVA model replying in the same language as the query (Image-induced Fidelity Loss).
Replacing the monolingual language backbone (Vicuna) with a bilingual one (Yi or Leo) reduces IFL.
Visual inputs are mapped to a distinct region of the embedding space, separate from text embeddings of any language.
A simple mechanistic intervention (adding a language attribute vector to an intermediate layer) can substantially reduce IFL.
papers.limitation:
The debiased results rely on the assumption that the expert-annotated gold standard is correct, which may not be the case, especially for unfamiliar scripts.
The UMAP visualizations showing separation between image and text embeddings do not definitively prove they are mapped to distinct semantic spaces.
The study aggregates results across languages and does not focus on second- and third-order interactions or heterogeneous patterns of IFL between languages.
future_direction: Improving the mechanistic intervention through automatic attribute selection or better attribute construction.
Studying the broader class of fidelity loss in single-modality models.
Better understanding the heterogeneous patterns of IFL across languages.
papers.abstract: We uncover a surprising multilingual bias occurring in a popular class of multimodal vision-language models (VLMs). Including an image in the query to a LLaVA-style VLM significantly increases the likelihood of the model returning an English response, regardless of the language of the query. This paper investigates the causes of this loss with a two-pronged approach that combines extensive ablation of the design space with a mechanistic analysis of the models' internal representations of image and text inputs. Both approaches indicate that the issue stems in the language modelling component of the LLaVA model. Statistically, we find that switching the language backbone for a bilingual language model has the strongest effect on reducing this error. Mechanistically, we provide compelling evidence that visual inputs are not mapped to a similar space as text ones, and that intervening on intermediary attention layers can reduce this bias. Our findings provide important insights to researchers and engineers seeking to understand the crossover between multimodal and multilingual spaces, and contribute to the goal of developing capable and inclusive VLMs for non-English contexts.

papers.title: The Semantic Hub Hypothesis: Language Models Share Semantic Representations Across Languages and Modalities
papers.research_question: To what extent do language models learn and use a shared semantic representation space across different languages and modalities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the semantic hub hypothesis, which posits that language models learn a shared representation space across languages and modalities, and provides evidence through representation similarity and intervention experiments.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models learn a shared semantic representation space (the semantic hub) that is anchored by the dominant language and is causally involved in processing across languages and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
Model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in intermediate layers.
The shared representation space is scaffolded by the model's dominant language (e.g., English) and can be interpreted via the logit lens.
This phenomenon extends to other data types: arithmetic expressions, code, images, and audio.
Interventions in the shared space using the dominant language affect model outputs in other data types, indicating causal usage.
The shared space is not just a byproduct but actively used during processing.
papers.limitation:
Chameleon-7B cannot answer more sophisticated reasoning questions about images, such as asking for a country flag or spatial relationships, even without interventions.
The logit lens analysis for audio is a lower bound because many words in labels (e.g., prepositions) are unlikely to be represented in the audio hidden states.
future_direction: Future work aimed at better controlling models using insights from the semantic hub hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can process inputs across diverse languages and modalities. We hypothesize that models acquire this capability through learning a shared representation space across heterogeneous data types (e.g., different languages and modalities), which places semantically similar inputs near one another, even if they are from different modalities/languages. We term this the semantic hub hypothesis, following the hub-and-spoke model from neuroscience (Patterson et al., 2007) which posits that semantic knowledge in the human brain is organized through a transmodal semantic "hub" which integrates information from various modality-specific "spokes" regions. We first show that model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in the intermediate layers, and that this space can be interpreted using the model's dominant pretraining language via the logit lens. This tendency extends to other data types, including arithmetic expressions, code, and visual/audio inputs. Interventions in the shared representation space in one data type also predictably affect model outputs in other data types, suggesting that this shared representations space is not simply a vestigial byproduct of large-scale training on broad data, but something that is actively utilized by the model during input processing.

papers.title: Do Multilingual Neural Machine Translation Models Contain Language Pair Specific Attention Heads?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual neural machine translation models contain language pair specific attention heads? The paper investigates this by analyzing individual attention heads in a many-to-one NMT model.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that in a multilingual NMT model, the most important attention heads are largely language-independent, and about 30% of heads can be pruned without significant performance loss.
papers.conclusion: Although rare language-pair specific attention heads exist, the most important heads are language-independent, and around 30% of heads can be pruned without retraining and with almost no loss in BLEU.
papers.key_findings:
The set of most important attention heads is very similar across different language pairs.
It is possible to remove nearly one-third of the less important attention heads without greatly hurting translation quality.
For encoder-decoder (cross) attention heads, the coverage metric is a better indicator for pruning importance, while for encoder self-attention heads, the confidence metric is more effective.
Some rare attention heads are language-pair specific, as identified by the exhaustive Sequential Backward Selection (SBS) procedure.
The variance, confidence, and coverage metrics provide a proxy for head importance, but the SBS algorithm yields the best ranking for pruning.
future_direction: Perform pruning at different levels of granularity (beyond single scalar metrics) to identify which parts of the model are more language-specific.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on the analysis of the multilingual representations focus on identifying whether there is an emergence of languageindependent representations, or whether a multilingual model partitions its weights among different languages. While most of such work has been conducted in a "black-box" manner, this paper aims to analyze individual components of a multilingual neural translation (NMT) model. In particular, we look at the encoder self-attention and encoder-decoder attention heads (in a many-to-one NMT model) that are more specific to the translation of a certain language pair than others by (1) employing metrics that quantify some aspects of the attention weights such as "variance" or "confidence", and (2) systematically ranking the importance of attention heads with respect to translation quality. Experimental results show that surprisingly, the set of most important attention heads are very similar across the language pairs and that it is possible to remove nearly one-third of the less important heads without hurting the translation quality greatly.

papers.title: Identifying and Controlling Important Neurons in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How important are individual neurons for obtaining high-quality translations? Do individual neurons in NMT models contain interpretable linguistic information? Can we control MT output by intervening in the representation at the individual neuron level?
papers.core_contribution: Develops unsupervised methods (MaxCorr, MinCorr, LinReg, SVCCA) for discovering important neurons in NMT models, shows these neurons impact translation quality and capture linguistic phenomena, and demonstrates translation control by modifying individual neuron activations.
papers.conclusion: The work indicates that not all information is distributed in NMT models, and many human-interpretable grammatical and structural properties are captured by individual neurons. Modifying neuron activations allows for controlling translation output according to specified linguistic properties.
papers.key_findings:
Erasing top-ranked neurons (by the proposed methods) hurts translation quality more than erasing bottom-ranked neurons.
Individual neurons capture interpretable linguistic properties such as parentheses, tense, number, gender, and noun phrase segmentation.
Translation output can be controlled (e.g., tense, number, gender) by modifying the activations of specific neurons, though success varies by property.
Different ranking methods capture different types of information: MaxCorr and MinCorr tend to find position information, while LinReg and SVCCA find token identity information.
The methods are task-independent and can be applied to other neural networks.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is applied only to LSTM-based NMT models; application to other architectures like the Transformer is left for future work.
Controlling some properties (e.g., gender) is more difficult, possibly because they are more distributed than others (e.g., tense).
future_direction: Apply the analysis to other NMT components (e.g., the decoder) and architectures (e.g., Transformer, convolutional sequence-to-sequence).
Develop more sophisticated ways to control translation output, for example by modifying representations in variational NMT architectures.
Analyze the spectrum of localized vs. distributed information in neural language representations more broadly.
papers.abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) models learn representations containing substantial linguistic information. However, it is not clear if such information is fully distributed or if some of it can be attributed to individual neurons. We develop unsupervised methods for discovering important neurons in NMT models. Our methods rely on the intuition that different models learn similar properties, and do not require any costly external supervision. We show experimentally that translation quality depends on the discovered neurons, and find that many of them capture common linguistic phenomena. Finally, we show how to control NMT translations in predictable ways, by modifying activations of individual neurons.

papers.title: Entangled in Representations: Mechanistic Investigation of Cultural Biases in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are cultural biases, such as Western-dominance bias and cultural flattening, internalized and represented within the parameters of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Culturescope, a mechanistic interpretability method to probe internal representations of cultural knowledge, and finds that LLMs internalize Western-dominance bias and cultural flattening, with low-resource cultures being less susceptible due to limited parametric knowledge.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a foundation for future research on mitigating cultural biases and enhancing LLMs' cultural understanding, suggesting that tailored approaches considering both bias and resource levels are needed.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs internalize Western-dominance bias and cultural flattening in their cultural knowledge space.
Low-resource cultures are less susceptible to cultural biases, likely due to the model's limited parametric knowledge about them.
The Cultural Flattening (CF) score and attention contribution scores reveal asymmetric generalization of culturally distinctive knowledge, often aligned with geographic or cultural proximity.
When models answer cultural questions incorrectly, they show a statistically significant preference for biased options (hard negatives) for mid- and high-resource cultures, but not for low-resource cultures.
Culturescope effectively surfaces relevant cultural knowledge from model representations, as validated by relevance evaluation and irrelevant patching tests.
papers.limitation:
Few existing benchmarks are suitable for the evaluation setup, requiring a consistent QA format across cultures; the methods inherit limitations from the benchmarks such as lack of fine-grained cultures and a 1-to-1 mapping of culture and country.
Due to computational constraints, experiments are limited to 8B parameter models.
future_direction: Future work should develop tailored approaches that consider the impact of bias and resource levels to improve LLMs' cultural understanding.
Future research should aim at mitigating internalized cultural biases and developing culturally aligned LLMs.
papers.abstract: The growing deployment of large language models (LLMs) across diverse cultural contexts necessitates a deeper understanding of LLMs' representations of different cultures. Prior work has focused on evaluating the cultural awareness of LLMs by only examining the text they generate. This approach overlooks the internal sources of cultural misrepresentation within the models themselves. To bridge this gap, we propose Culturescope, the first mechanistic interpretability-based method that probes the internal representations of different cultural knowledge in LLMs. We also introduce a cultural flattening score as a measure of the intrinsic cultural biases of the decoded knowledge from Culturescope. Additionally, we study how LLMs internalize cultural biases, which allows us to trace how cultural biases such as Western-dominance bias and cultural flattening emerge within LLMs. We find that low-resource cultures are less susceptible to cultural biases, likely due to the model's limited parametric knowledge. Our work provides a foundation for future research on mitigating cultural biases and enhancing LLMs' cultural understanding.

papers.title: Focusing on Language: Revealing and Exploiting Language Attention Heads in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the role of multi-head self-attention in supporting multilingual processing in LLMs? Specifically, are there language-specific and language-general attention heads, and how can they be used to control model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LAHIS, a method to identify language-specific and language-general attention heads in multilingual LLMs, and shows how modulating these heads can control cross-lingual attention and improve multilingual performance with minimal parameters.
papers.conclusion: The work enhances interpretability of multilingual behaviors in LLMs from the perspective of MHA and presents practical approaches to strengthen multilingual capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
LAHIS reveals the existence of language-specific and language-general attention heads in multilingual LLMs.
Language-specific heads enable cross-lingual attention transfer, allowing steering of model attention to target languages.
Modulating language-specific heads mitigates off-target language generation by suppressing English-heads.
A lightweight adaptation using a trainable matrix on language-specific heads improves multilingual question answering accuracy with only 14-20 parameters.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support multilingual understanding and generation. Meanwhile, efforts to interpret their internal mechanisms have emerged, offering insights to enhance multilingual performance. While multi-head self-attention (MHA) has proven critical in many areas, its role in multilingual capabilities remains underexplored. In this work, we study the contribution of MHA in supporting multilingual processing in LLMs. We propose Language Attention Head Importance Scores (LAHIS), an effective and efficient method that identifies attention head importance for multilingual capabilities via a single forward and backward pass through the LLM. Applying LAHIS to Aya-23-8B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Mistral-7B-v0.1, we reveal the existence of both language-specific and language-general heads. Language-specific heads enable cross-lingual attention transfer to guide the model toward target language contexts and mitigate off-target language generation issue, contributing to addressing challenges in multilingual LLMs. We also introduce a lightweight adaptation that learns a soft head mask to modulate attention outputs over language heads, requiring only 20 tunable parameters to improve XQuAD accuracy. Overall, our work enhances both the interpretability and multilingual capabilities of LLMs from the perspective of MHA.

papers.title: Deep Subjecthood: Higher-Order Grammatical Features in Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: How does Multilingual BERT (mBERT) encode abstract grammatical features like morphosyntactic alignment, and is subjecthood represented as a discrete or continuous category?
papers.core_contribution: mBERT encodes high-level grammatical features like morphosyntactic alignment in its contextual embeddings, and subjecthood is represented as a continuous, probabilistic concept influenced by semantic and discourse factors.
papers.conclusion: mBERT encodes abstract grammatical features like morphosyntactic alignment in its contextual embeddings, and subjecthood is represented as a continuous, probabilistic concept influenced by both syntax and semantics.
papers.key_findings:
Classifiers trained to distinguish transitive subjects (A) and objects (O) from mBERT embeddings achieve high accuracy, peaking in middle layers (7-10).
When tested on intransitive subjects (S), classifier predictions reflect the morphosyntactic alignment of the training language: classifiers trained on ergative languages are more likely to classify S as O.
Zero-shot cross-lingual transfer of subjecthood classification is successful, indicating parallel encoding of grammatical relations across languages in mBERT.
Classifier decisions are influenced by semantic and syntactic factors: passive subjects are ambiguous, animate nouns are more likely to be classified as agents, and case markings affect classification.
mBERT's representation of subjecthood is continuous and probabilistic, aligning with functional linguistics theories rather than being a purely discrete syntactic category.
papers.limitation: The Universal Dependencies training data and mBERT training languages are heavily weighted towards nominative-accusative languages, leading to a nominative-accusative bias and noisy results due to limited ergative language data.
future_direction: Examine the effects of balanced joint training between nominative-accusative and ergative-absolutive languages on the contextual embedding of subjecthood.
Continue investigating how deep neural models represent discrete linguistic features probabilistically.
papers.abstract: We investigate how Multilingual BERT (mBERT) encodes grammar by examining how the high-order grammatical feature of morphosyntactic alignment (how different languages define what counts as a "subject") is manifested across the embedding spaces of different languages. To understand if and how morphosyntactic alignment affects contextual embedding spaces, we train classifiers to recover the subjecthood of mBERT embeddings in transitive sentences (which do not contain overt information about morphosyntactic alignment) and then evaluate them zero-shot on intransitive sentences (where subjecthood classification depends on alignment), within and across languages. We find that the resulting classifier distributions reflect the morphosyntactic alignment of their training languages. Our results demonstrate that mBERT representations are influenced by high-level grammatical features that are not manifested in any one input sentence, and that this is robust across languages. Further examining the characteristics that our classifiers rely on, we find that features such as passive voice, animacy and case strongly correlate with classification decisions, suggesting that mBERT does not encode subjecthood purely syntactically, but that subjecthood embedding is continuous and dependent on semantic and discourse factors, as is proposed in much of the functional linguistics literature. Together, these results provide insight into how grammatical features manifest in contextual embedding spaces, at a level of abstraction not covered by previous work.

papers.title: A multilabel approach to morphosyntactic probing
papers.research_question: How well does multilingual BERT encode morphosyntactic features across languages, and which features are recognized as shared cross-linguistically?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a multilabel probing paradigm for morphosyntactic analysis and demonstrates that multilingual BERT encodes many morphosyntactic features extractably, with some features shared cross-linguistically.
papers.conclusion: Multilabel probing is an effective method for analyzing morphosyntactic representations in multilingual language models, revealing that mBERT encodes many features and that some are represented cross-linguistically.
papers.key_findings:
mBERT-6 holds the most morphosyntactic information, with probes achieving micro-averaged F1 scores between 0.83 and 0.97 for seven languages.
Multilingual probes slightly underperform monolingual probes but exhibit better selectivity, suggesting less memorization.
Cross-lingual transfer experiments show that nouns and verbs are well transferred, while adjectives and nominative case are less consistently recognized across languages.
The multilabel paradigm enables fine-grained analysis of feature co-occurrence and agreement patterns, as demonstrated in a case study of Hebrew determiners.
Probe performance varies across languages due to differences in feature sets and training set sizes, making direct comparison difficult.
papers.limitation: The UD corpora used are from narrow domains (e.g., Wikipedia, news, Bible) and may not capture the full range of linguistic phenomena.
future_direction: Probe different multilingual language models to compare their morphosyntactic representations.
Explore how global and feature-level probe performance corresponds to downstream task performance.
Conduct more detailed analyses of specific features and their cross-linguistic transfer.
papers.abstract: We propose using a multilabel probing task to assess the morphosyntactic representations of multilingual word embeddings. This tweak on canonical probing makes it easy to explore morphosyntactic representations, both holistically and at the level of individual features (e.g., gender, number, case), and leads more naturally to the study of how language models handle co-occurring features (e.g., agreement phenomena). We demonstrate this task with multilingual BERT Through this simple but robust paradigm, we verify that multilingual BERT renders many morphosyntactic features simultaneously extractable. We further evaluate the probes on six held-out languages: Arabic, Chinese, Marathi, Slovenian, Tagalog, and Yorb. This zero-shot style of probing has the added benefit of revealing which cross-linguistic properties a language model recognizes as being shared by multiple languages.

papers.title: From Monolingual to Bilingual: Investigating Language Conditioning in Large Language Models for Psycholinguistic Tasks
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages, and how does language identity (monolingual vs bilingual prompting) affect their output behavior and internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that large language models condition their psycholinguistic behavior and internal representations on the language identity specified in the prompt, with differences between monolingual and bilingual prompting, offering insights into cross-linguistic cognition in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our results demonstrate that LLMs are not language-neutral. Instead, they respond to and encode language-specific cues in both their outputs and internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Both models adapt their outputs based on the linguistic identity embedded in the prompt.
Qwen shows greater sensitivity to prompt language and sharper behavioral distinctions between Dutch and Chinese than Llama.
Probing reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more linearly decodable in deeper layers.
Chinese prompts yield stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch prompts.
Bilingual prompting can introduce interference or noise, especially for low-resource languages like Dutch.
papers.limitation:
Focus on only three languages (English, Dutch, Chinese), limiting generalizability.
Only two LLMs are evaluated.
Tasks represent only a narrow slice of the psycholinguistic space.
future_direction: Expanding to include languages with different scripts, phonological systems, or morphological complexity (e.g., Arabic, Hindi, Finnish).
Incorporating a broader set of psycholinguistic phenomena, such as lexical decision making, semantic priming, syntactic ambiguity resolution, and metaphor comprehension.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong linguistic capabilities, but little is known about how they encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages. We investigate whether and how LLMs exhibit human-like psycholinguistic responses under different linguistic identities using two tasks: sound symbolism and word valence. We evaluate two models, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, under monolingual and bilingual prompting in English, Dutch, and Chinese. Behaviorally, both models adjust their outputs based on prompted language identity, with Qwen showing greater sensitivity and sharper distinctions between Dutch and Chinese. Probing analysis reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more decodable in deeper layers, with Chinese prompts yielding stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch. Our results demonstrate that language identity conditions both output behavior and internal representations in LLMs, providing new insights into their application as models of cross-linguistic cognition.

papers.title: Local Contrastive Editing of Gender Stereotypes
papers.research_question: How can we localize individual weights that drive stereotypical gender bias in language models and modify these weights to steer and mitigate the bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces local contrastive editing, a two-step method to localize and edit a small subset (<0.5%) of model weights that encode gender bias, enabling flexible control and mitigation of bias while largely preserving model performance.
papers.conclusion: Stereotypical gender bias is encoded in specific subsets of weights within language models, and local contrastive editing can effectively identify and modify these subsets to control and mitigate bias.
papers.key_findings:
A very small subset (<0.5%) of model weights is responsible for encoding stereotypical gender bias.
Local contrastive editing strategies (interpolation, extrapolation, pruning) can successfully steer and mitigate gender bias in a controlled manner.
The identified bias-encoding weights are concentrated in higher layers of the transformer, particularly in the attention output dense layer.
Editing based on strategic localization is crucial; uninformed editing of random weights does not effectively change bias.
The method preserves the model's language modeling ability and downstream task performance, except for value-based pruning which degrades performance.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted using a single model architecture (BERT) and a single type of bias (gender bias).
Computational constraints limit the scope of experiments, as iterative magnitude pruning requires substantial resources.
The study uses a binary specification of gender (male/female), which does not encompass the full gender spectrum.
future_direction: Explore application of local contrastive editing to other tasks and domains beyond gender bias.
papers.abstract: Stereotypical bias encoded in language models (LMs) poses a threat to safe language technology, yet our understanding of how bias manifests in the parameters of LMs remains incomplete. We introduce local contrastive editing that enables the localization and editing of a subset of weights in a target model in relation to a reference model. We deploy this approach to identify and modify subsets of weights that are associated with gender stereotypes in LMs. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate that local contrastive editing can precisely localize and control a small subset (< 0.5%) of weights that encode gender bias. Our work (i) advances our understanding of how stereotypical biases can manifest in the parameter space of LMs and (ii) opens up new avenues for developing parameter-efficient strategies for controlling model properties in a contrastive manner.

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of Morphological Content in BERT Models for Multiple Languages
papers.research_question: To what extent do BERT-style models encode morphological feature information in their hidden representations and attention distributions for multiple languages?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that BERT-style models encode morphological information by partitioning their embedding space into convex regions correlated with feature values, that contextualized embeddings help disambiguate ambiguous forms but not completely, and that specific attention head/layer combinations focus on subject-verb agreement.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that pre-trained BERT-style models are sensitive to morphological information, with strong performance on feature-value classification and certain attention heads learning to focus attention in a manner consistent with morphological agreement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-style models partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value.
Contextualized embeddings allow models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases.
Specific attention head/layer combinations hone in on subject-verb agreement.
Supervision significantly aids in extracting morphological information, as unsupervised clustering performs near random baselines.
Morphological information is best represented in the middle layers for languages with complex morphology (German and Russian), while for simpler languages it is present throughout all layers.
papers.limitation:
Models have difficulty disambiguating syncretic (ambiguous) forms, especially in languages with complex inflectional morphology.
The classification tasks require supervision; unsupervised methods (k-means) perform near random baselines.
future_direction: Identifying morphological information in BERT-style models in an unsupervised fashion.
Improving models' ability to disambiguate syncretic forms for languages with complex inflectional morphology.
Further exploration of how morphological information is shared between words via self-attention.
