CLAS is not uniformly beneficial and can cause performance regressions for some languages.
Mechanistic analysis does not isolate attention heads or other circuit components, limiting causal attribution.
future_direction: Explore adaptive steering strategies based on representational structure.
Better understand saturation effects in well-separated language clusters.
Extend CLAS to other modalities and training settings.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit strong multilingual capabilities, yet significant performance gaps persist between dominant and non-dominant languages. Prior work attributes this gap to imbalances between shared and language-specific neurons in multilingual representations. We propose Cross-Lingual Activation Steering (CLAS), a training-free inference-time intervention that selectively modulates neuron activations. We evaluate CLAS on classification and generation benchmarks, achieving average improvements of 2.3% (Acc.) and 3.4% (F1) respectively, while maintaining high-resource language performance. We discover that effective transfer operates through functional divergence rather than strict alignment; performance gains correlate with increased language cluster separation. Our results demonstrate that targeted activation steering can unlock latent multilingual capacity in existing models without modification to model weights.

papers.title: Investigating Bias Representations in Llama 2 Chat via Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How does activation steering reveal and mitigate societal biases in Llama 2 7B Chat, and what does this say about the model's internal representations of bias?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering uncovers inherent gender bias in Llama 2 7B Chat and shows that RLHF leads to increased similarity in the model's representation of different societal biases, suggesting a loss of nuanced understanding.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering is effective for red-teaming biases in LLMs, and RLHF may cause the model to conflate different bias types, reducing nuanced understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Llama 2 7B Chat exhibits inherent gender bias despite undergoing Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF).
Bias steering vectors trigger refusal responses, and subtracting a refusal vector can elicit biased outputs from the model.
Bias vectors are transferable across dimensions; for example, racial bias steering can elicit gender and religion bias.
There is a negative correlation between bias vectors and refusal vectors, as shown by cosine similarity across layers.
RLHF increases the cosine similarity between different bias vectors in the Chat model compared to the base model, indicating that biases become more closely associated.
papers.abstract: We address the challenge of societal bias in Large Language Models (LLMs), focusing on the Llama 2 7B Chat model. As LLMs are increasingly integrated into decision-making processes with substantial societal impact, it becomes imperative to ensure these models do not reinforce existing biases. Our approach employs activation steering to probe for and mitigate biases related to gender, race, and religion. This method manipulates model activations to direct responses towards or away from biased outputs, utilizing steering vectors derived from the StereoSet dataset and custom GPT4 generated gender bias prompts. Our findings reveal inherent gender bias in Llama 2 7B Chat, persisting even after Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). We also observe a predictable negative correlation between bias and the model's tendency to refuse responses. Significantly, our study uncovers that RLHF tends to increase the similarity in the model's representation of different forms of societal biases, which raises questions about the model's nuanced understanding of different forms of bias. This work also provides valuable insights into effective red-teaming strategies for LLMs using activation steering, particularly emphasizing the importance of integrating a refusal vector.

papers.title: Why do LLaVA Vision-Language Models Reply to Images in English?
papers.research_question: Why do LLaVA-style vision-language models tend to reply in English when an image is included in the query, regardless of the query language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes Image-induced Fidelity Loss (IFL) in LLaVA models, finding the bias originates in the language backbone and can be mitigated by using bilingual language models or through a mechanistic intervention on intermediate attention layers.
papers.conclusion: Image-induced Fidelity Loss is a significant issue in LLaVA models, localized within the language model component. Improving the multilinguality of the underlying LLM is a promising path for building more robust multilingual VLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Adding an image to a query significantly reduces the probability of a LLaVA model replying in the same language as the query (Image-induced Fidelity Loss).
Replacing the monolingual language backbone (Vicuna) with a bilingual one (Yi or Leo) reduces IFL.
Visual inputs are mapped to a distinct region of the embedding space, separate from text embeddings of any language.
A simple mechanistic intervention (adding a language attribute vector to an intermediate layer) can substantially reduce IFL.
papers.limitation:
The debiased results rely on the assumption that the expert-annotated gold standard is correct, which may not be the case, especially for unfamiliar scripts.
The UMAP visualizations showing separation between image and text embeddings do not definitively prove they are mapped to distinct semantic spaces.
The study aggregates results across languages and does not focus on second- and third-order interactions or heterogeneous patterns of IFL between languages.
future_direction: Improving the mechanistic intervention through automatic attribute selection or better attribute construction.
Studying the broader class of fidelity loss in single-modality models.
Better understanding the heterogeneous patterns of IFL across languages.
papers.abstract: We uncover a surprising multilingual bias occurring in a popular class of multimodal vision-language models (VLMs). Including an image in the query to a LLaVA-style VLM significantly increases the likelihood of the model returning an English response, regardless of the language of the query. This paper investigates the causes of this loss with a two-pronged approach that combines extensive ablation of the design space with a mechanistic analysis of the models' internal representations of image and text inputs. Both approaches indicate that the issue stems in the language modelling component of the LLaVA model. Statistically, we find that switching the language backbone for a bilingual language model has the strongest effect on reducing this error. Mechanistically, we provide compelling evidence that visual inputs are not mapped to a similar space as text ones, and that intervening on intermediary attention layers can reduce this bias. Our findings provide important insights to researchers and engineers seeking to understand the crossover between multimodal and multilingual spaces, and contribute to the goal of developing capable and inclusive VLMs for non-English contexts.

papers.title: The Semantic Hub Hypothesis: Language Models Share Semantic Representations Across Languages and Modalities
papers.research_question: To what extent do language models learn and use a shared semantic representation space across different languages and modalities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the semantic hub hypothesis, which posits that language models learn a shared representation space across languages and modalities, and provides evidence through representation similarity and intervention experiments.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models learn a shared semantic representation space (the semantic hub) that is anchored by the dominant language and is causally involved in processing across languages and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
Model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in intermediate layers.
The shared representation space is scaffolded by the model's dominant language (e.g., English) and can be interpreted via the logit lens.
This phenomenon extends to other data types: arithmetic expressions, code, images, and audio.
Interventions in the shared space using the dominant language affect model outputs in other data types, indicating causal usage.
The shared space is not just a byproduct but actively used during processing.
papers.limitation:
Chameleon-7B cannot answer more sophisticated reasoning questions about images, such as asking for a country flag or spatial relationships, even without interventions.
The logit lens analysis for audio is a lower bound because many words in labels (e.g., prepositions) are unlikely to be represented in the audio hidden states.
future_direction: Future work aimed at better controlling models using insights from the semantic hub hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can process inputs across diverse languages and modalities. We hypothesize that models acquire this capability through learning a shared representation space across heterogeneous data types (e.g., different languages and modalities), which places semantically similar inputs near one another, even if they are from different modalities/languages. We term this the semantic hub hypothesis, following the hub-and-spoke model from neuroscience (Patterson et al., 2007) which posits that semantic knowledge in the human brain is organized through a transmodal semantic "hub" which integrates information from various modality-specific "spokes" regions. We first show that model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in the intermediate layers, and that this space can be interpreted using the model's dominant pretraining language via the logit lens. This tendency extends to other data types, including arithmetic expressions, code, and visual/audio inputs. Interventions in the shared representation space in one data type also predictably affect model outputs in other data types, suggesting that this shared representations space is not simply a vestigial byproduct of large-scale training on broad data, but something that is actively utilized by the model during input processing.

papers.title: Do Multilingual Neural Machine Translation Models Contain Language Pair Specific Attention Heads?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual neural machine translation models contain language pair specific attention heads? The paper investigates this by analyzing individual attention heads in a many-to-one NMT model.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that in a multilingual NMT model, the most important attention heads are largely language-independent, and about 30% of heads can be pruned without significant performance loss.
papers.conclusion: Although rare language-pair specific attention heads exist, the most important heads are language-independent, and around 30% of heads can be pruned without retraining and with almost no loss in BLEU.
papers.key_findings:
The set of most important attention heads is very similar across different language pairs.
It is possible to remove nearly one-third of the less important attention heads without greatly hurting translation quality.
For encoder-decoder (cross) attention heads, the coverage metric is a better indicator for pruning importance, while for encoder self-attention heads, the confidence metric is more effective.
Some rare attention heads are language-pair specific, as identified by the exhaustive Sequential Backward Selection (SBS) procedure.
The variance, confidence, and coverage metrics provide a proxy for head importance, but the SBS algorithm yields the best ranking for pruning.
future_direction: Perform pruning at different levels of granularity (beyond single scalar metrics) to identify which parts of the model are more language-specific.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on the analysis of the multilingual representations focus on identifying whether there is an emergence of languageindependent representations, or whether a multilingual model partitions its weights among different languages. While most of such work has been conducted in a "black-box" manner, this paper aims to analyze individual components of a multilingual neural translation (NMT) model. In particular, we look at the encoder self-attention and encoder-decoder attention heads (in a many-to-one NMT model) that are more specific to the translation of a certain language pair than others by (1) employing metrics that quantify some aspects of the attention weights such as "variance" or "confidence", and (2) systematically ranking the importance of attention heads with respect to translation quality. Experimental results show that surprisingly, the set of most important attention heads are very similar across the language pairs and that it is possible to remove nearly one-third of the less important heads without hurting the translation quality greatly.

papers.title: Identifying and Controlling Important Neurons in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How important are individual neurons for obtaining high-quality translations? Do individual neurons in NMT models contain interpretable linguistic information? Can we control MT output by intervening in the representation at the individual neuron level?
papers.core_contribution: Develops unsupervised methods (MaxCorr, MinCorr, LinReg, SVCCA) for discovering important neurons in NMT models, shows these neurons impact translation quality and capture linguistic phenomena, and demonstrates translation control by modifying individual neuron activations.
papers.conclusion: The work indicates that not all information is distributed in NMT models, and many human-interpretable grammatical and structural properties are captured by individual neurons. Modifying neuron activations allows for controlling translation output according to specified linguistic properties.
papers.key_findings:
Erasing top-ranked neurons (by the proposed methods) hurts translation quality more than erasing bottom-ranked neurons.
Individual neurons capture interpretable linguistic properties such as parentheses, tense, number, gender, and noun phrase segmentation.
Translation output can be controlled (e.g., tense, number, gender) by modifying the activations of specific neurons, though success varies by property.
Different ranking methods capture different types of information: MaxCorr and MinCorr tend to find position information, while LinReg and SVCCA find token identity information.
The methods are task-independent and can be applied to other neural networks.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is applied only to LSTM-based NMT models; application to other architectures like the Transformer is left for future work.
Controlling some properties (e.g., gender) is more difficult, possibly because they are more distributed than others (e.g., tense).
future_direction: Apply the analysis to other NMT components (e.g., the decoder) and architectures (e.g., Transformer, convolutional sequence-to-sequence).
Develop more sophisticated ways to control translation output, for example by modifying representations in variational NMT architectures.
Analyze the spectrum of localized vs. distributed information in neural language representations more broadly.
papers.abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) models learn representations containing substantial linguistic information. However, it is not clear if such information is fully distributed or if some of it can be attributed to individual neurons. We develop unsupervised methods for discovering important neurons in NMT models. Our methods rely on the intuition that different models learn similar properties, and do not require any costly external supervision. We show experimentally that translation quality depends on the discovered neurons, and find that many of them capture common linguistic phenomena. Finally, we show how to control NMT translations in predictable ways, by modifying activations of individual neurons.

papers.title: Entangled in Representations: Mechanistic Investigation of Cultural Biases in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are cultural biases, such as Western-dominance bias and cultural flattening, internalized and represented within the parameters of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Culturescope, a mechanistic interpretability method to probe internal representations of cultural knowledge, and finds that LLMs internalize Western-dominance bias and cultural flattening, with low-resource cultures being less susceptible due to limited parametric knowledge.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a foundation for future research on mitigating cultural biases and enhancing LLMs' cultural understanding, suggesting that tailored approaches considering both bias and resource levels are needed.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs internalize Western-dominance bias and cultural flattening in their cultural knowledge space.
Low-resource cultures are less susceptible to cultural biases, likely due to the model's limited parametric knowledge about them.
The Cultural Flattening (CF) score and attention contribution scores reveal asymmetric generalization of culturally distinctive knowledge, often aligned with geographic or cultural proximity.
When models answer cultural questions incorrectly, they show a statistically significant preference for biased options (hard negatives) for mid- and high-resource cultures, but not for low-resource cultures.
Culturescope effectively surfaces relevant cultural knowledge from model representations, as validated by relevance evaluation and irrelevant patching tests.
papers.limitation:
Few existing benchmarks are suitable for the evaluation setup, requiring a consistent QA format across cultures; the methods inherit limitations from the benchmarks such as lack of fine-grained cultures and a 1-to-1 mapping of culture and country.
Due to computational constraints, experiments are limited to 8B parameter models.
future_direction: Future work should develop tailored approaches that consider the impact of bias and resource levels to improve LLMs' cultural understanding.
Future research should aim at mitigating internalized cultural biases and developing culturally aligned LLMs.
papers.abstract: The growing deployment of large language models (LLMs) across diverse cultural contexts necessitates a deeper understanding of LLMs' representations of different cultures. Prior work has focused on evaluating the cultural awareness of LLMs by only examining the text they generate. This approach overlooks the internal sources of cultural misrepresentation within the models themselves. To bridge this gap, we propose Culturescope, the first mechanistic interpretability-based method that probes the internal representations of different cultural knowledge in LLMs. We also introduce a cultural flattening score as a measure of the intrinsic cultural biases of the decoded knowledge from Culturescope. Additionally, we study how LLMs internalize cultural biases, which allows us to trace how cultural biases such as Western-dominance bias and cultural flattening emerge within LLMs. We find that low-resource cultures are less susceptible to cultural biases, likely due to the model's limited parametric knowledge. Our work provides a foundation for future research on mitigating cultural biases and enhancing LLMs' cultural understanding.

papers.title: Focusing on Language: Revealing and Exploiting Language Attention Heads in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the role of multi-head self-attention in supporting multilingual processing in LLMs? Specifically, are there language-specific and language-general attention heads, and how can they be used to control model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LAHIS, a method to identify language-specific and language-general attention heads in multilingual LLMs, and shows how modulating these heads can control cross-lingual attention and improve multilingual performance with minimal parameters.
papers.conclusion: The work enhances interpretability of multilingual behaviors in LLMs from the perspective of MHA and presents practical approaches to strengthen multilingual capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
LAHIS reveals the existence of language-specific and language-general attention heads in multilingual LLMs.
Language-specific heads enable cross-lingual attention transfer, allowing steering of model attention to target languages.
Modulating language-specific heads mitigates off-target language generation by suppressing English-heads.
A lightweight adaptation using a trainable matrix on language-specific heads improves multilingual question answering accuracy with only 14-20 parameters.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support multilingual understanding and generation. Meanwhile, efforts to interpret their internal mechanisms have emerged, offering insights to enhance multilingual performance. While multi-head self-attention (MHA) has proven critical in many areas, its role in multilingual capabilities remains underexplored. In this work, we study the contribution of MHA in supporting multilingual processing in LLMs. We propose Language Attention Head Importance Scores (LAHIS), an effective and efficient method that identifies attention head importance for multilingual capabilities via a single forward and backward pass through the LLM. Applying LAHIS to Aya-23-8B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Mistral-7B-v0.1, we reveal the existence of both language-specific and language-general heads. Language-specific heads enable cross-lingual attention transfer to guide the model toward target language contexts and mitigate off-target language generation issue, contributing to addressing challenges in multilingual LLMs. We also introduce a lightweight adaptation that learns a soft head mask to modulate attention outputs over language heads, requiring only 20 tunable parameters to improve XQuAD accuracy. Overall, our work enhances both the interpretability and multilingual capabilities of LLMs from the perspective of MHA.

papers.title: Deep Subjecthood: Higher-Order Grammatical Features in Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: How does Multilingual BERT (mBERT) encode abstract grammatical features like morphosyntactic alignment, and is subjecthood represented as a discrete or continuous category?
papers.core_contribution: mBERT encodes high-level grammatical features like morphosyntactic alignment in its contextual embeddings, and subjecthood is represented as a continuous, probabilistic concept influenced by semantic and discourse factors.
papers.conclusion: mBERT encodes abstract grammatical features like morphosyntactic alignment in its contextual embeddings, and subjecthood is represented as a continuous, probabilistic concept influenced by both syntax and semantics.
papers.key_findings:
Classifiers trained to distinguish transitive subjects (A) and objects (O) from mBERT embeddings achieve high accuracy, peaking in middle layers (7-10).
When tested on intransitive subjects (S), classifier predictions reflect the morphosyntactic alignment of the training language: classifiers trained on ergative languages are more likely to classify S as O.
Zero-shot cross-lingual transfer of subjecthood classification is successful, indicating parallel encoding of grammatical relations across languages in mBERT.
Classifier decisions are influenced by semantic and syntactic factors: passive subjects are ambiguous, animate nouns are more likely to be classified as agents, and case markings affect classification.
mBERT's representation of subjecthood is continuous and probabilistic, aligning with functional linguistics theories rather than being a purely discrete syntactic category.
papers.limitation: The Universal Dependencies training data and mBERT training languages are heavily weighted towards nominative-accusative languages, leading to a nominative-accusative bias and noisy results due to limited ergative language data.
future_direction: Examine the effects of balanced joint training between nominative-accusative and ergative-absolutive languages on the contextual embedding of subjecthood.
Continue investigating how deep neural models represent discrete linguistic features probabilistically.
papers.abstract: We investigate how Multilingual BERT (mBERT) encodes grammar by examining how the high-order grammatical feature of morphosyntactic alignment (how different languages define what counts as a "subject") is manifested across the embedding spaces of different languages. To understand if and how morphosyntactic alignment affects contextual embedding spaces, we train classifiers to recover the subjecthood of mBERT embeddings in transitive sentences (which do not contain overt information about morphosyntactic alignment) and then evaluate them zero-shot on intransitive sentences (where subjecthood classification depends on alignment), within and across languages. We find that the resulting classifier distributions reflect the morphosyntactic alignment of their training languages. Our results demonstrate that mBERT representations are influenced by high-level grammatical features that are not manifested in any one input sentence, and that this is robust across languages. Further examining the characteristics that our classifiers rely on, we find that features such as passive voice, animacy and case strongly correlate with classification decisions, suggesting that mBERT does not encode subjecthood purely syntactically, but that subjecthood embedding is continuous and dependent on semantic and discourse factors, as is proposed in much of the functional linguistics literature. Together, these results provide insight into how grammatical features manifest in contextual embedding spaces, at a level of abstraction not covered by previous work.

papers.title: A multilabel approach to morphosyntactic probing
papers.research_question: How well does multilingual BERT encode morphosyntactic features across languages, and which features are recognized as shared cross-linguistically?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a multilabel probing paradigm for morphosyntactic analysis and demonstrates that multilingual BERT encodes many morphosyntactic features extractably, with some features shared cross-linguistically.
papers.conclusion: Multilabel probing is an effective method for analyzing morphosyntactic representations in multilingual language models, revealing that mBERT encodes many features and that some are represented cross-linguistically.
papers.key_findings:
mBERT-6 holds the most morphosyntactic information, with probes achieving micro-averaged F1 scores between 0.83 and 0.97 for seven languages.
Multilingual probes slightly underperform monolingual probes but exhibit better selectivity, suggesting less memorization.
Cross-lingual transfer experiments show that nouns and verbs are well transferred, while adjectives and nominative case are less consistently recognized across languages.
The multilabel paradigm enables fine-grained analysis of feature co-occurrence and agreement patterns, as demonstrated in a case study of Hebrew determiners.
Probe performance varies across languages due to differences in feature sets and training set sizes, making direct comparison difficult.
papers.limitation: The UD corpora used are from narrow domains (e.g., Wikipedia, news, Bible) and may not capture the full range of linguistic phenomena.
future_direction: Probe different multilingual language models to compare their morphosyntactic representations.
Explore how global and feature-level probe performance corresponds to downstream task performance.
Conduct more detailed analyses of specific features and their cross-linguistic transfer.
papers.abstract: We propose using a multilabel probing task to assess the morphosyntactic representations of multilingual word embeddings. This tweak on canonical probing makes it easy to explore morphosyntactic representations, both holistically and at the level of individual features (e.g., gender, number, case), and leads more naturally to the study of how language models handle co-occurring features (e.g., agreement phenomena). We demonstrate this task with multilingual BERT Through this simple but robust paradigm, we verify that multilingual BERT renders many morphosyntactic features simultaneously extractable. We further evaluate the probes on six held-out languages: Arabic, Chinese, Marathi, Slovenian, Tagalog, and Yorb. This zero-shot style of probing has the added benefit of revealing which cross-linguistic properties a language model recognizes as being shared by multiple languages.

papers.title: From Monolingual to Bilingual: Investigating Language Conditioning in Large Language Models for Psycholinguistic Tasks
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages, and how does language identity (monolingual vs bilingual prompting) affect their output behavior and internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that large language models condition their psycholinguistic behavior and internal representations on the language identity specified in the prompt, with differences between monolingual and bilingual prompting, offering insights into cross-linguistic cognition in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our results demonstrate that LLMs are not language-neutral. Instead, they respond to and encode language-specific cues in both their outputs and internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Both models adapt their outputs based on the linguistic identity embedded in the prompt.
Qwen shows greater sensitivity to prompt language and sharper behavioral distinctions between Dutch and Chinese than Llama.
Probing reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more linearly decodable in deeper layers.
Chinese prompts yield stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch prompts.
Bilingual prompting can introduce interference or noise, especially for low-resource languages like Dutch.
papers.limitation:
Focus on only three languages (English, Dutch, Chinese), limiting generalizability.
Only two LLMs are evaluated.
Tasks represent only a narrow slice of the psycholinguistic space.
future_direction: Expanding to include languages with different scripts, phonological systems, or morphological complexity (e.g., Arabic, Hindi, Finnish).
Incorporating a broader set of psycholinguistic phenomena, such as lexical decision making, semantic priming, syntactic ambiguity resolution, and metaphor comprehension.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong linguistic capabilities, but little is known about how they encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages. We investigate whether and how LLMs exhibit human-like psycholinguistic responses under different linguistic identities using two tasks: sound symbolism and word valence. We evaluate two models, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, under monolingual and bilingual prompting in English, Dutch, and Chinese. Behaviorally, both models adjust their outputs based on prompted language identity, with Qwen showing greater sensitivity and sharper distinctions between Dutch and Chinese. Probing analysis reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more decodable in deeper layers, with Chinese prompts yielding stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch. Our results demonstrate that language identity conditions both output behavior and internal representations in LLMs, providing new insights into their application as models of cross-linguistic cognition.

papers.title: Local Contrastive Editing of Gender Stereotypes
papers.research_question: How can we localize individual weights that drive stereotypical gender bias in language models and modify these weights to steer and mitigate the bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces local contrastive editing, a two-step method to localize and edit a small subset (<0.5%) of model weights that encode gender bias, enabling flexible control and mitigation of bias while largely preserving model performance.
papers.conclusion: Stereotypical gender bias is encoded in specific subsets of weights within language models, and local contrastive editing can effectively identify and modify these subsets to control and mitigate bias.
papers.key_findings:
A very small subset (<0.5%) of model weights is responsible for encoding stereotypical gender bias.
Local contrastive editing strategies (interpolation, extrapolation, pruning) can successfully steer and mitigate gender bias in a controlled manner.
The identified bias-encoding weights are concentrated in higher layers of the transformer, particularly in the attention output dense layer.
Editing based on strategic localization is crucial; uninformed editing of random weights does not effectively change bias.
The method preserves the model's language modeling ability and downstream task performance, except for value-based pruning which degrades performance.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted using a single model architecture (BERT) and a single type of bias (gender bias).
Computational constraints limit the scope of experiments, as iterative magnitude pruning requires substantial resources.
The study uses a binary specification of gender (male/female), which does not encompass the full gender spectrum.
future_direction: Explore application of local contrastive editing to other tasks and domains beyond gender bias.
papers.abstract: Stereotypical bias encoded in language models (LMs) poses a threat to safe language technology, yet our understanding of how bias manifests in the parameters of LMs remains incomplete. We introduce local contrastive editing that enables the localization and editing of a subset of weights in a target model in relation to a reference model. We deploy this approach to identify and modify subsets of weights that are associated with gender stereotypes in LMs. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate that local contrastive editing can precisely localize and control a small subset (< 0.5%) of weights that encode gender bias. Our work (i) advances our understanding of how stereotypical biases can manifest in the parameter space of LMs and (ii) opens up new avenues for developing parameter-efficient strategies for controlling model properties in a contrastive manner.

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of Morphological Content in BERT Models for Multiple Languages
papers.research_question: To what extent do BERT-style models encode morphological feature information in their hidden representations and attention distributions for multiple languages?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that BERT-style models encode morphological information by partitioning their embedding space into convex regions correlated with feature values, that contextualized embeddings help disambiguate ambiguous forms but not completely, and that specific attention head/layer combinations focus on subject-verb agreement.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that pre-trained BERT-style models are sensitive to morphological information, with strong performance on feature-value classification and certain attention heads learning to focus attention in a manner consistent with morphological agreement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-style models partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value.
Contextualized embeddings allow models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases.
Specific attention head/layer combinations hone in on subject-verb agreement.
Supervision significantly aids in extracting morphological information, as unsupervised clustering performs near random baselines.
Morphological information is best represented in the middle layers for languages with complex morphology (German and Russian), while for simpler languages it is present throughout all layers.
papers.limitation:
Models have difficulty disambiguating syncretic (ambiguous) forms, especially in languages with complex inflectional morphology.
The classification tasks require supervision; unsupervised methods (k-means) perform near random baselines.
future_direction: Identifying morphological information in BERT-style models in an unsupervised fashion.
Improving models' ability to disambiguate syncretic forms for languages with complex inflectional morphology.
Further exploration of how morphological information is shared between words via self-attention.
papers.abstract: This work describes experiments which probe the hidden representations of several BERT-style models for morphological content. The goal is to examine the extent to which discrete linguistic structure, in the form of morphological features and feature values, presents itself in the vector representations and attention distributions of pre-trained language models for five European languages. The experiments contained herein show that (i) Transformer architectures largely partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value, (ii) the contextualized nature of transformer embeddings allows models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases, and (iii) very specific attention head/layer combinations appear to hone in on subject-verb agreement.

papers.title: Finding Universal Grammatical Relations in Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: To what extent does Multilingual BERT learn a cross-lingual representation of syntactic structure? Does mBERT learn universal grammatical relations without explicit supervision?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual BERT learns cross-lingual syntactic representations; its syntactic subspaces are shared across languages and capture dependency clusters that largely agree with the Universal Dependencies taxonomy, indicating the model induces universal grammatical relations without explicit supervision.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual BERT learns cross-lingual syntactic representations and induces universal grammatical relations without explicit supervision, which largely agree with the dependency labels of Universal Dependencies.
papers.key_findings:
The structural probe recovers syntactic tree distances in multiple languages from mBERT representations.
The syntactic subspaces are shared across languages, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer of syntactic information.
mBERT represents dependency clusters that largely overlap with the Universal Dependencies taxonomy, showing it learns universal grammatical relations.
The cross-lingual syntactic subspace is a small part (approx. 32-128 dimensions) of the overall 768-dimensional representation.
Transfer probe performance is substantially correlated with subspace similarity across languages.
papers.limitation:
Cannot tease apart whether transfer performance is caused by subword overlap or by a more fundamental sharing of parameters.
Only conduct a qualitative study in the unsupervised emergence of dependency labels via t-SNE; future work could extend to quantitative results.
Acknowledge issues in interpreting t-SNE plots.
Methods cannot support causal implications for the decisions made by the model.
future_direction: Explore other multilingual models like XLM and XLM-RoBERTa.
Attempt to understand the extent to which the discovered properties have causal implications for the model's decisions.
papers.abstract: Recent work has found evidence that Multilingual BERT (mBERT), a transformer-based multilingual masked language model, is capable of zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, suggesting that some aspects of its representations are shared cross-lingually. To better understand this overlap, we extend recent work on finding syntactic trees in neural networks' internal representations to the multilingual setting. We show that subspaces of mBERT representations recover syntactic tree distances in languages other than English, and that these subspaces are approximately shared across languages. Motivated by these results, we present an unsupervised analysis method that provides evidence mBERT learns representations of syntactic dependency labels, in the form of clusters which largely agree with the Universal Dependencies taxonomy. This evidence suggests that even without explicit supervision, multilingual masked language models learn certain linguistic universals.

papers.title: Interpreting Bias in Large Language Models: A Feature-Based Approach
papers.research_question: How do biases propagate in large language models, and how can they be interpreted and mitigated using a feature-based approach?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a feature-based method for analyzing and mitigating gender bias in LLMs, identifying the roles of MLPs and attention heads in bias propagation, and demonstrating targeted debiasing using counterfactual datasets.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a novel feature-based approach for interpreting and mitigating gender bias in LLMs, showing that targeted interventions can reduce bias and providing insights into bias mechanisms for future ethical AI development.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias in LLMs originates in early layers, primarily through MLPs, as shown by activation patching experiments.
Attention heads copy bias from profession tokens to final token positions, propagating bias through the network, validated via attribution patching.
Targeted debiasing by fine-tuning identified components (MLPs or attention heads) can reduce bias, but effectiveness varies across models and may be limited by dataset size.
The feature-based approach is extensible to other forms of gender bias, such as stereotypes in household duties, by mapping features to model components.
Patching MLP outputs or attention heads can reverse biased logit orders without losing profession information in generated text, indicating selective intervention.
papers.limitation:
Potential compensation phenomenon where other components take over after patching, which may affect analysis.
Restricted to English language bias only, limiting generalizability.
The approach may require case-by-case tweaking, which is not scalable for multiple biases.
future_direction: Exploring bias interactions in multilingual settings
Examining the impact of debiasing across languages from a white-box perspective
Investigating applicability to other areas like AI security and alignment
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) such as Mistral and LLaMA have showcased remarkable performance across various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Despite their success, these models inherit social biases from the diverse datasets on which they are trained. This paper investigates the propagation of biases within LLMs through a novel feature-based analytical approach. Drawing inspiration from causal mediation analysis, we hypothesize the evolution of bias-related features and validate them using interpretability techniques like activation and attribution patching. Our contributions are threefold: (1) We introduce and empirically validate a feature-based method for bias analysis in LLMs, applied to LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-3-8B, and Mistral-7B-v0.3 with templates from a professions dataset. (2) We extend our method to another form of gender bias, demonstrating its generalizability. (3) We differentiate the roles of MLPs and attention heads in bias propagation and implement targeted debiasing using a counterfactual dataset. Our findings reveal the complex nature of bias in LLMs and emphasize the necessity for tailored debiasing strategies, offering a deeper understanding of bias mechanisms and pathways for effective mitigation.

papers.title: Debiasing Algorithm through Model Adaptation
papers.research_question: Can we identify evidence of gender bias in LLaMA? Can we identify which components store the gender-biased representation? Can we edit the model's weights to decrease bias while preserving performance on end-tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DAMA, a method to debias language models by identifying bias-mediating components via causal tracing and editing their weights via linear projection, significantly reducing gender bias while preserving performance.
papers.conclusion: DAMA effectively reduces gender bias in LLaMA models by editing weights of bias-mediating MLP layers, with minimal impact on general language understanding and task performance.
papers.key_findings:
LLaMA models exhibit gender bias in language generation, coreference resolution, and sentence completion.
Mid-upper MLP layers are the primary mediators of gender bias in LLaMA models.
DAMA significantly reduces gender bias across multiple metrics (language generation, WinoBias, StereoSet).
DAMA maintains the model's performance on language modeling and downstream tasks (ARC, OBQA, MMLU) with minimal degradation.
The method is effective across different model sizes (7B, 13B, 30B, 65B).
papers.limitation: The method's effectiveness may depend on the choice of layers and projection dimensions, requiring hyperparameter tuning.
future_direction: Improve the method of finding projection matrices, possibly using convex search or analytically derived pseudo-projections.
Investigate further the ranges of layers and dimensions that convey bias to apply DAMA effectively on other model types.
Extend the approach to other languages, particularly morphologically rich languages with more ubiquitous gender marking.
papers.abstract: Large language models are becoming the go-to solution for the ever-growing number of tasks. However, with growing capacity, models are prone to rely on spurious correlations stemming from biases and stereotypes present in the training data. This work proposes a novel method for detecting and mitigating gender bias in language models. We perform causal analysis to identify problematic model components and discover that mid-upper feed-forward layers are most prone to convey bias. Based on the analysis results, we intervene in the model by applying a linear projection to the weight matrices of these layers. Our titular method, DAMA, significantly decreases bias as measured by diverse metrics while maintaining the model's performance on downstream tasks. We release code for our method and models, which retrain LLaMA's state-of-the-art performance while being significantly less biased.

papers.title: Tokenization and Morphology in Multilingual Language Models: A Comparative Analysis of mT5 and ByT5
papers.research_question: How does tokenization influence the morphological knowledge encoded in multilingual language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper finds that tokenization strategies (subword vs. character-level) affect how morphological knowledge is encoded in multilingual language models, with differences across languages and tasks, and that morphological information is best represented in middle to late layers.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that tokenization influences morphological knowledge encoding, with no clear advantage of character-level over subword tokenization, and highlights the importance of considering morphological complexity and training data proportions.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual language models learn the morphological systems of some languages better than others.
Morphological information is encoded in the middle and late layers of the models.
Character-level models (ByT5) capture morphological knowledge later than subword models (mT5), but achieve similar overall performance.
The degree of morphological irregularity in a language amplifies the effect of training data size on probing accuracy.
Different morphological tasks (number, tense, case, gender) are learned with varying difficulty, with case being the hardest.
papers.limitation:
Orthographic transparency is not taken into account.
Experiments were run only once due to high volume.
The dataset is biased towards Indo-European languages.
Focus is only on inflectional morphology, not derivational.
P-values should be treated with care due to large sample size.
future_direction: Why tense and case features are challenging for character-based models is a question for future research.
papers.abstract: Morphology is a crucial factor for multilingual language modeling as it poses direct challenges for tokenization. Here, we seek to understand how tokenization influences the morphological knowledge encoded in multilingual language models. Specifically, we capture the impact of tokenization by contrasting two multilingual language models: mT5 and ByT5. The two models share the same architecture, training objective, and training data and only differ in their tokenization strategies: subword tokenization vs.\@ character-level tokenization. Probing the morphological knowledge encoded in these models on four tasks and 17 languages, our analyses show that the models learn the morphological systems of some languages better than others and that morphological information is encoded in the middle and late layers. Finally, we show that languages with more irregularities benefit more from having a higher share of the pre-training data.

papers.title: GECOBench: a gender-controlled text dataset and benchmark for quantifying biases in explanations
papers.research_question: What is the explanation performance of widely adopted XAI methods given word-level ground truth feature attributions, and how does gender bias in pre-trained models affect this performance depending on fine-tuning strategies?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces GECO, a gender-controlled text dataset, and GECOBench, a benchmarking framework to evaluate the correctness of feature attribution methods, showing that fine-tuning embedding layers mitigates gender bias in explanations.
papers.conclusion: GECO and GECOBench provide a controlled framework for benchmarking feature attribution methods, revealing that fine-tuning embedding layers can mitigate gender bias in explanations, though the task is a simplification of real-world gender diversity.
papers.key_findings:
Explanation performance varies across different XAI methods.
Fine-tuning or retraining embedding layers of BERT improves the correctness of feature attributions.
Gender bias contained in pre-trained language models negatively affects data-centric explanation performance.
The OLA model, trained from scratch on the GECO dataset, achieves higher explanation performance than fine-tuned BERT variants.
The proposed benchmark enables quantitative assessment of explanation bias and the impact of fine-tuning strategies.
papers.limitation:
The gender classification task is a simplification that does not reflect the full spectrum of gender identities.
The dataset is based on Wikipedia articles of classic novels, which may contain historical gender norms.
The study is limited to the BERT model and a specific gender classification task.
future_direction: Extend the framework to more diverse text sources and richer notions of gender.
Apply the benchmark to broader fairness concepts and more complex tasks.
Investigate the impact of different pre-training corpora and model architectures.
papers.abstract: Large pre-trained language models have become a crucial backbone for many downstream tasks in natural language processing (NLP), and while they are trained on a plethora of data containing a variety of biases, such as gender biases, it has been shown that they can also inherit such biases in their weights, potentially affecting their prediction behavior. However, it is unclear to what extent these biases also affect feature attributions generated by applying "explainable artificial intelligence" (XAI) techniques, possibly in unfavorable ways. To systematically study this question, we create a gender-controlled text dataset, GECO, in which the alteration of grammatical gender forms induces class-specific words and provides ground truth feature attributions for gender classification tasks. This enables an objective evaluation of the correctness of XAI methods. We apply this dataset to the pre-trained BERT model, which we fine-tune to different degrees, to quantitatively measure how pre-training induces undesirable bias in feature attributions and to what extent fine-tuning can mitigate such explanation bias. To this extent, we provide GECOBench, a rigorous quantitative evaluation framework for benchmarking popular XAI methods. We show a clear dependency between explanation performance and the number of fine-tuned layers, where XAI methods are observed to benefit particularly from fine-tuning or complete retraining of embedding layers.

papers.title: Discriminating Form and Meaning in Multilingual Models with Minimal-Pair ABX Tasks
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models represent language identity (form) and semantic content (meaning), and how do these representations evolve during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a training-free ABX-style discrimination framework for analyzing multilingual representations, and shows that in XLM-R, language discrimination decreases and concentrates in lower layers over training, while meaning discrimination increases and stabilizes in deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: ABX discrimination metrics provide a lightweight, interpretable tool for analyzing multilingual representations, revealing that language discrimination decreases and concentrates in lower layers while meaning discrimination increases in deeper layers, with implications for understanding cross-lingual transfer.
papers.key_findings:
Language discrimination declines over training and becomes concentrated in lower layers.
Meaning discrimination strengthens over time and stabilizes in deeper layers.
There is a negative correlation between language and meaning discrimination across language pairs and checkpoints.
Language discrimination negatively correlates with performance on form-sensitive tasks like POS and NER in cross-lingual transfer.
Meaning discrimination does not consistently predict downstream task performance.
papers.limitation:
Encoder architecture and single-model scope: only tested on XLM-R (encoder-only), not decoder-only or encoder-decoder models.
Discrimination vs Separation: does not explicitly quantify separation in the representation space.
Task coverage: only POS, NER, NLI, may not capture deeper semantic capabilities.
Cross-linguistic generality vs. language-specific phenomena: not investigating specific languages or families in detail.
future_direction: Linking discrimination patterns to typological linguistic features.
Evaluating deeper semantic tasks.
Applying ABX metrics to decoder-only LLMs and more recent multilingual models.
papers.abstract: We introduce a set of training-free ABX-style discrimination tasks to evaluate how multilingual language models represent language identity (form) and semantic content (meaning). Inspired from speech processing, these zero-shot tasks measure whether minimal differences in representation can be reliably detected. This offers a flexible and interpretable alternative to probing. Applied to XLM-R (Conneau et al, 2020) across pretraining checkpoints and layers, we find that language discrimination declines over training and becomes concentrated in lower layers, while meaning discrimination strengthens over time and stabilizes in deeper layers. We then explore probing tasks, showing some alignment between our metrics and linguistic learning performance. Our results position ABX tasks as a lightweight framework for analyzing the structure of multilingual representations.

papers.title: How Do Multilingual Language Models Remember Facts?
papers.research_question: How do factual recall mechanisms in English LLMs generalize to multilingual LLMs, and when does language play a role in recall?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that factual recall mechanisms in multilingual LLMs share similarities with English LLMs but with key differences, such as the role of MLPs in extraction and the composition of relation and language in the last token's function vector.
papers.conclusion: These insights reveal unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for recalling information, highlighting the need for new methodologies—such as knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition—that are specifically tailored for multilingual LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Previously identified recall mechanisms in English largely apply to multilingual contexts, with nuances based on language and architecture.
Subject enrichment is language-independent, while object extraction is language-dependent.
The last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV), encoding both the language of the query and the content to be extracted.
In decoder-only LLMs, FVs compose relation and language in two separate stages.
MLPs play a more prominent role in extraction in multilingual LLMs compared to English LLMs.
papers.limitation: Excluded languages with too few examples, limiting the analysis to a subset of languages.
future_direction: Developing new methodologies for knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition tailored for multilingual LLMs
Studying whether models 'think' in English by examining how the function vector is altered across languages
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) store and retrieve vast amounts of factual knowledge acquired during pre-training. Prior research has localized and identified mechanisms behind knowledge recall; however, it has only focused on English monolingual models. The question of how these mechanisms generalize to non-English languages and multilingual LLMs remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap by conducting a comprehensive analysis of three multilingual LLMs. First, we show that previously identified recall mechanisms in English largely apply to multilingual contexts, with nuances based on language and architecture. Next, through patching intermediate representations, we localize the role of language during recall, finding that subject enrichment is language-independent, while object extraction is language-dependent. Additionally, we discover that the last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV), encoding both the language of the query and the content to be extracted from the subject. Furthermore, in decoder-only LLMs, FVs compose these two pieces of information in two separate stages. These insights reveal unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for recalling information, highlighting the need for new methodologies -- such as knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition -- that are specifically tailored for multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: Interpreting Arithmetic Mechanism in Large Language Models through Comparative Neuron Analysis
papers.research_question: How is arithmetic ability implemented in large language models, specifically the role of attention heads and FFN neurons, and what is the internal logic chain from input to prediction? Additionally, how does the LoRA fine-tuning method work?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Comparative Neuron Analysis (CNA) method to interpret arithmetic mechanisms in LLMs, identifying an internal logic chain of four stages, and applies it to understand LoRA and for model pruning and bias reduction.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies important attention heads and FFN neurons for arithmetic, proposes the CNA method to construct the internal logic chain, finds LoRA amplifies important FFN neurons, and applies CNA to model pruning and editing.
papers.key_findings:
Arithmetic ability is localized in a few attention heads (arithmetic heads), each specializing in distinct operations.
The internal logic chain from input to prediction consists of four stages: feature enhancing, feature transferring, feature predicting, and prediction enhancing.
LoRA enhances prediction probabilities by amplifying the coefficient scores of important FFN neurons related to the final prediction.
Model pruning retaining only 5% of deep FFN neurons identified by CNA maintains performance on arithmetic tasks.
Model editing by zeroing 18 FFN neurons identified by CNA reduces gender bias by 35.7%.
papers.limitation:
The case studies rely on projecting vectors in vocabulary space, which is empirically interpretable but lacks complete theoretical foundation.
There is a lack of standardization across various studies regarding attribution methods (e.g., different intervention methods).
A potential risk is that attackers can identify and edit important neurons to change model behavior maliciously.
future_direction: Further investigation of the multiplication heads which do not significantly impact accuracy.
Explorations on different datasets for gender bias reduction.
Distinguishing whether a model has been edited to prevent malicious use.

papers.title: Models of Visually Grounded Speech Signal Pay Attention to Nouns: A Bilingual Experiment on English and Japanese
papers.research_question: What is the behavior of attention in neural models of visually grounded speech trained on English and Japanese, and does it focus on nouns?
papers.core_contribution: Shows that attention in neural models of visually grounded speech focuses on nouns across English and Japanese, and demonstrates cross-lingual speech retrieval using images as pivots.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that attention in visually grounded speech models focuses on nouns across languages, with language-specific adaptations, and enables cross-lingual retrieval using images as pivots.
papers.key_findings:
Attention primarily focuses on nouns in both English and Japanese models.
The Japanese model also pays attention to particles, developing a language-specific behavior similar to human toddlers.
Attention peaks are located at word endings in English and at both beginnings and endings in Japanese.
Images can be used as pivots for cross-lingual speech-to-speech retrieval without parallel data.
The model exhibits noun-bias, aligning with theories of child language acquisition.
papers.limitation: The study uses synthetic speech with only one voice, whereas prior work used real speech with multiple speakers.
future_direction: Validate the methodology on a bilingual dataset featuring real voices.
Extract a bilingual speech-to-speech dictionary using attention peaks as anchor points.
papers.abstract: We investigate the behaviour of attention in neural models of visually grounded speech trained on two languages: English and Japanese. Experimental results show that attention focuses on nouns and this behaviour holds true for two very typologically different languages. We also draw parallels between artificial neural attention and human attention and show that neural attention focuses on word endings as it has been theorised for human attention. Finally, we investigate how two visually grounded monolingual models can be used to perform cross-lingual speech-to-speech retrieval. For both languages, the enriched bilingual (speech-image) corpora with part-of-speech tags and forced alignments are distributed to the community for reproducible research.

papers.title: Semantic and Structural Analysis of Implicit Biases in Large Language Models: An Interpretable Approach
papers.research_question: How to identify and explain implicit stereotypes in large language models using an interpretable bias detection method?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an interpretable bias detection method for large language models that integrates nested semantic representation with attention perturbation to identify hidden social biases in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The interpretable detection method effectively identifies implicit biases in LLMs, improving detection accuracy and semantic consistency, and provides a foundation for bias intervention and ethical deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method achieves higher bias detection accuracy (84.7%), semantic consistency (91.2%), and lower contextual sensitivity (8.5) compared to baselines.
It demonstrates strong generalization across multiple stereotype dimensions, with higher accuracy for gender and profession than for religion and race.
Higher semantic similarity between texts leads to more consistent bias judgments, reducing conflict rates.
Attention perturbation analysis reveals the model's sensitivity to social attribute terms, helping uncover bias pathways.
The method provides interpretable insights into how implicit stereotypes are formed in language models.
papers.limitation: Performance declines on more complex, culturally embedded biases such as religion and race due to their subtlety and ambiguity.
future_direction: Expand the method's adaptability to cross-cultural and multilingual contexts.
Integrate external knowledge bases and user feedback signals for more flexible bias detection.
Embed interpretability mechanisms into model interaction interfaces for user perception and response.
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the issue of implicit stereotypes that may arise during the generation process of large language models. It proposes an interpretable bias detection method aimed at identifying hidden social biases in model outputs, especially those semantic tendencies that are not easily captured through explicit linguistic features. The method combines nested semantic representation with a contextual contrast mechanism. It extracts latent bias features from the vector space structure of model outputs. Using attention weight perturbation, it analyzes the model's sensitivity to specific social attribute terms, thereby revealing the semantic pathways through which bias is formed. To validate the effectiveness of the method, this study uses the StereoSet dataset, which covers multiple stereotype dimensions including gender, profession, religion, and race. The evaluation focuses on several key metrics, such as bias detection accuracy, semantic consistency, and contextual sensitivity. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves strong detection performance across various dimensions. It can accurately identify bias differences between semantically similar texts while maintaining high semantic alignment and output stability. The method also demonstrates high interpretability in its structural design. It helps uncover the internal bias association mechanisms within language models. This provides a more transparent and reliable technical foundation for bias detection. The approach is suitable for real-world applications where high trustworthiness of generated content is required.

papers.title: Contributions of Transformer Attention Heads in Multi- and Cross-lingual Tasks
papers.research_question: What are the effects of pruning attention heads in multilingual Transformer-based models on cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks, and how can important heads be identified?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that pruning a subset of attention heads in multilingual Transformer models (mBERT and XLM-R) generally improves performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual sequence labeling tasks, and introduces a gradient-based method to rank and identify which heads to prune.
papers.conclusion: Pruning attention heads in multilingual Transformer models generally improves performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual sequence labeling tasks, and the gradient-based method effectively identifies heads to prune, offering better model interpretability and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning attention heads in mBERT and XLM-R generally has positive effects on model performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual sequence labeling tasks (POS, NER, SF).
A gradient-based method can effectively rank attention heads by importance, and pruning the lowest-ranked heads leads to performance improvements.
The important attention heads for a task are shared across languages, as evidenced by high correlation in head rankings across different languages.
Pruning attention heads is beneficial even when training data in the target language is limited, making models more applicable to resource-poor languages.
In multi-source language settings, pruning attention heads also improves performance, and the gradient-based ranking method can be extended to multiple source languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to sequence labeling tasks (POS, NER, SF) and may not generalize to other cross-lingual tasks.
future_direction: Improving model interpretability in other cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks, e.g., XNLI and other passage-level classification tasks.
papers.abstract: Weicheng Ma, Kai Zhang, Renze Lou, Lili Wang, Soroush Vosoughi. Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2021.

papers.title: Race, Ethnicity and Their Implication on Bias in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are race and ethnicity represented and operationalized within large language models, and what are the internal mechanisms underlying demographic bias?
papers.core_contribution: We provide a mechanistic analysis of how race and ethnicity are represented in LLMs, showing that demographic information is distributed across internal units and that bias mitigation requires more than manipulating a few neurons.
papers.conclusion: Mitigating demographic bias in LLMs requires not only outcome-level interventions but also a deeper examination of representational structure and task-dependent reuse.
papers.key_findings:
Demographic information is distributed across many internal units rather than localized to a small set of neurons.
Models decompose race and ethnicity into multiple, interpretable semantic facets such as explicit group labels and associated geographic or linguistic attributes.
Stereotype-related and historically harmful associations are present across models despite differences in training data.
Interventions suppressing race-encoding neurons reduce bias but leave substantial residual effects, indicating behavioral rather than representational change.
Direct and indirect demographic cues activate different internal representations, influencing model behavior differently.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly operate in high-stakes settings including healthcare and medicine, where demographic attributes such as race and ethnicity may be explicitly stated or implicitly inferred from text. However, existing studies primarily document outcome-level disparities, offering limited insight into internal mechanisms underlying these effects. We present a mechanistic study of how race and ethnicity are represented and operationalized within LLMs. Using two publicly available datasets spanning toxicity-related generation and clinical narrative understanding tasks, we analyze three open-source models with a reproducible interpretability pipeline combining probing, neuron-level attribution, and targeted intervention. We find that demographic information is distributed across internal units with substantial cross-model variation. Although some units encode sensitive or stereotype-related associations from pretraining, identical demographic cues can induce qualitatively different behaviors. Interventions suppressing such neurons reduce bias but leave substantial residual effects, suggesting behavioral rather than representational change and motivating more systematic mitigation.

papers.title: LFTF: Locating First and Then Fine-Tuning for Mitigating Gender Bias in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we effectively mitigate gender bias in Large Language Models (LLMs) by locating and fine-tuning the most bias-related model components while preserving general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces two datasets (GenBiasEval, GenHintEval) and corresponding metrics (AFGB-Score, UB-Score) for evaluating gender bias in LLMs, and proposes the LFTF algorithm which locates bias-related blocks using a BMI metric and fine-tunes them with a novel loss function to mitigate bias while preserving general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: The proposed LFTF algorithm, along with the new evaluation datasets and metrics, effectively mitigates gender bias in LLMs while maintaining their general capabilities, as demonstrated through extensive experiments.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed LFTF algorithm significantly reduces gender bias (as measured by AFGB-Score) on multiple LLMs (Qwen2.5-7B, Meta-Llama3-8B, Vicuna-7B-v1.5).
LFTF maintains the model's ability to respond correctly to prompts containing gender hints (as measured by UB-Score).
LFTF preserves general capabilities on most benchmark tasks (e.g., MMLU, code generation), with only a slight decline observed on mathematical reasoning tasks.
Existing model editing methods (ROME, MEND, MEMIT) fail for debiasing as they turn the model into an 'anti-bias' model, performing poorly on both bias and hint evaluation.
The Block Mitigating Importance (BMI) score effectively identifies the last block of the tested models as the most strongly associated with gender bias.
papers.limitation: The GenBiasEval dataset is based on work that assumes a binary gender model (male/female).
future_direction: Extending the evaluation datasets and the LFTF method to other social biases such as race, age, and religious bias.
papers.abstract: Nowadays, Large Language Models (LLMs) have attracted widespread attention due to their powerful performance. However, due to the unavoidable exposure to socially biased data during training, LLMs tend to exhibit social biases, particularly gender bias. To better explore and quantifying the degree of gender bias in LLMs, we propose a pair of datasets named GenBiasEval and GenHintEval, respectively. The GenBiasEval is responsible for evaluating the degree of gender bias in LLMs, accompanied by an evaluation metric named AFGB-Score (Absolutely Fair Gender Bias Score). Meanwhile, the GenHintEval is used to assess whether LLMs can provide responses consistent with prompts that contain gender hints, along with the accompanying evaluation metric UB-Score (UnBias Score). Besides, in order to mitigate gender bias in LLMs more effectively, we present the LFTF (Locating First and Then Fine-Tuning) algorithm.The algorithm first ranks specific LLM blocks by their relevance to gender bias in descending order using a metric called BMI (Block Mitigating Importance Score). Based on this ranking, the block most strongly associated with gender bias is then fine-tuned using a carefully designed loss function. Numerous experiments have shown that our proposed LFTF algorithm can significantly mitigate gender bias in LLMs while maintaining their general capabilities.

papers.title: Sharing Matters: Analysing Neurons Across Languages and Tasks in LLMs
papers.research_question: How is neuron activation shared across tasks and languages in multilingual large language models (LLMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a fine-grained neuron classification method for multilingual LLMs and demonstrates that neurons shared across all languages (all-shared neurons) are crucial for model performance and generating accurate responses.
papers.conclusion: The study improves understanding of the internal workings of multilingual LLMs by showing the pivotal role of cross-lingually shared neurons and the task- and model-dependent nature of neuron activation patterns, paving the way for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Deactivating all-shared neurons significantly decreases model performance across tasks (up to 87.39% drop in accuracy).
All-shared neurons have the greatest impact on generating both answers and correct answers, as measured by Generation Impact Score and Correctness Impact Score.
Neuron activation patterns vary across tasks, LLMs, and languages; for example, instruction-finetuned models show more all-shared neurons than foundation models.
Neuron sharing does not always align with language similarity; languages from the same family do not necessarily share more neurons.
Deactivating certain neuron types (partial-shared or specific) can occasionally improve performance for some languages, possibly due to mitigating knowledge conflicts.
future_direction: More in-depth investigation of how factual knowledge is stored and shared across languages in LLMs.
Further exploration of the relationship between language similarity and neuron sharing.
Investigation of whether in-context learning leads to better neuron activation composition rather than invoking more neurons.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized the field of natural language processing (NLP), and recent studies have aimed to understand their underlying mechanisms. However, most of this research is conducted within a monolingual setting, primarily focusing on English. Few studies have attempted to explore the internal workings of LLMs in multilingual settings. In this study, we aim to fill this research gap by examining how neuron activation is shared across tasks and languages. We classify neurons into four distinct categories based on their responses to a specific input across different languages: all-shared, partial-shared, specific, and non-activated. Building upon this categorisation, we conduct extensive experiments on three tasks across nine languages using several LLMs and present an in-depth analysis in this work. Our findings reveal that: (i) deactivating the all-shared neurons significantly decreases performance; (ii) the shared neurons play a vital role in generating responses, especially for the all-shared neurons; (iii) neuron activation patterns are highly sensitive and vary across tasks, LLMs, and languages. These findings shed light on the internal workings of multilingual LLMs and pave the way for future research. We release the code to foster research in this area.

papers.title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
papers.research_question: How can polysemantic interference structures in language models be exploited to manipulate model outputs, and do these interference patterns transfer across models of different scales and families?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that polysemantic interference structures in language models create a systematic vulnerability, and that interventions based on these structures, identified in small models, can transfer to larger instruction-tuned models for predictable behavioral control without requiring access to their internals.
papers.conclusion: Polysemantic interference reveals a systematic vulnerability in language models, and the generalization of these structures across scale and family challenges the view of polysemanticity as purely stochastic, offering new avenues for black-box control and theoretical insight into internal representation.
papers.key_findings:
Interventions leveraging polysemantic structures (feature-direction steering, token-gradient steering, prompt injection) can effectively manipulate model next-token predictions.
